claims.notes: De Soto's wintering place "most likely near present-day Tupelo" is Wikipedia's phrasing; the Chickasaw identification of that camp rests on the next paragraph of the article. Start year marks first documented European contact.

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek (20 October 1832), signed after Mississippi had extended its laws over them, the Chickasaw ceded their remaining homeland east of the Mississippi in exchange for a promise to find suitable land to the west.

citations.title: Treaty with the Chickasaw, 1832 (Treaty of Pontotoc Creek) - Chickasaw.tv
citations.quote: relinquished Chickasaw lands east of the Mississippi River in exchange for a promise to find suitable land west of the Mississippi River

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: ceding their remaining Mississippi territory to the U.S.

claims.notes: The Chickasaw Nation notes that settlers rushed in despite Article 15 of the treaty. A supplement was signed two days later.

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

claims.statement: The Chickasaw gathered at Memphis on 4 July 1837 and began their removal to Indian Territory, the last of the Five Tribes to leave the East; they settled within the Choctaw Nation under a treaty signed at Doaksville in 1837.

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Chickasaw gathered at Memphis, Tennessee, on July 4, 1837, with all of their portable assets

citations.title: A New Chahta Homeland: A History by the Decade, 1830-1840 - Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
citations.quote: Chickasaws were the last of the Five Tribes to leave their homeland in the East for Indian Territory.

citations.title: A New Chahta Homeland: A History by the Decade, 1830-1840 - Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
citations.quote: Choctaws and Chickasaws signed a treaty at Doaksville (near Fort Towson) to create a Chickasaw District within Choctaw Nation

claims.notes: Place = Pontotoc, the homeland removed from; removal continued through 1847 in several groups. The Chickasaw were separated from the Choctaw by treaty in 1855-56.

claims.statement: After a treaty signed in Washington in 1856 the Chickasaw Nation became independent in Indian Territory, with its capital at Tishomingo in what is now Oklahoma.

citations.title: Chickasaw Nation Capitols - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Nation became independent in 1856 when a treaty was signed in Washington giving the Chickasaw Nation full ownership of 4,707,903 acres of land

citations.title: Chickasaw Nation Capitols - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Tishomingo became the Nation's capital at this time

claims.notes: Wikipedia only for the capital date; the Chickasaw Nation remains headquartered in Oklahoma. A first constitution dates to 1848 and officers were elected in 1857 (same source).

place.name: Ackia and Ogoula Tchetoka (Chickasaw villages), Tupelo area, Mississippi

claims.statement: In 1736 French forces from Louisiana, with Choctaw and other allies, attacked fortified Chickasaw villages near present Tupelo, Mississippi, and were repulsed at Ogoula Tchetoka and Ackia.

citations.title: Battle of Ackia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Both attacks were bloodily repulsed

citations.title: Battle of Ackia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Ackia (in present-day south Tupelo, Mississippi) was attacked by the Southern force.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only. French and Chickasaw hostility continued after 1736. Coordinates are Tupelo (approximate; battle sites are in the Tupelo area).

place.name: Grand Village of the Natchez (Fatherland Site), Mississippi

claims.statement: The Grand Village (Fatherland Site) at present Natchez, Mississippi, was the main ceremonial and political centre of the Natchez and the home of the Great Sun from the time of La Salle's visit in 1682 until the Natchez abandoned it in 1730.

citations.title: Grand Village of the Natchez - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Between 1682 and 1729, the Natchez people used the village as their main ceremonial center, as noted in contemporary French accounts.

citations.title: Natchez Indians - 64 Parishes
citations.quote: A small mound center, Grand Village was the residence of chiefs known as "Great Sun" and "Tattooed Serpent."

claims.notes: Site construction began about 1200 CE by Plaquemine peoples (Wikipedia). Natchez settlements were a loose confederation (64 Parishes).

claims.statement: The French built Fort Rosalie in 1716 among the Natchez, anchoring a growing French settlement in Natchez country until, after the revolt of 1729, French and Choctaw reprisals in early 1730 forced the Natchez to abandon the fort.

citations.title: History & Culture - Natchez National Historical Park (NPS)
citations.quote: Established by the French among the Natchez people on the eastern bank of the Mississippi River in 1716

citations.title: Fort Rosalie - Wikipedia
citations.quote: French and allied Choctaw military reprisals in early 1730 forced the Natchez to abandon the fort, which was in ruins.

claims.notes: Fort Rosalie lies in the present city of Natchez; it was rebuilt by the French in the early 1730s.

place.name: Grand Village of the Natchez (Fatherland Site), Mississippi

claims.statement: After the 1729 revolt the French defeated the Natchez in 1730 and by 1731 had killed, captured or dispersed most of them; the Natchez abandoned the Grand Village and their homeland, ending the Natchez as a unified nation.

citations.title: Grand Village of the Natchez - Wikipedia
citations.quote: After suffering a military defeat by French settlers in 1730, the Natchez abandoned the site and moved away.

citations.title: Natchez Indians - 64 Parishes
citations.quote: The war ultimately led the Natchez to abandon their homeland.

citations.title: Fort Rosalie - Wikipedia
citations.quote: killing, capturing, or dispersing most of the Natchez, resulting in the end of the Natchez people as a unified political nation

claims.notes: Many were sold into slavery in Saint-Domingue; survivors took refuge among the Chickasaw, then the Creek and Cherokee, and their descendants live today within the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma (64 Parishes).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: The Catawba (Ye Iswa) occupied the Catawba River valley astride the present North Carolina-South Carolina border; the first recorded European contact was by Hernando de Soto in 1540.

citations.title: Catawba People - NCpedia
citations.quote: Historically, the American Indian people who came to be called "Catawba" occupied the Catawba River Valley above and below the present-day North Carolina-South Carolina border.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The first recorded contact with these people was by Hernando de Soto in 1540.

claims.notes: Coordinates are the Catawba Indian Nation reservation area (Wikidata point for the Catawba people); the original valley extended over a much larger area. The Catawba Nation absorbed refugees of about thirty other peoples after 1715 (NCpedia).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: The Catawba held a reservation fifteen miles square (about 144,000 acres) on the Catawba River in South Carolina, confirmed by the 1763 Treaty of Augusta, until the Treaty of Nation Ford in 1840.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the 1763 Treaty of Augusta ceded the Catawba tribe of South Carolina a tract of land "fifteen miles square" comprising approximately 144,000 acres

citations.title: Catawba People - NCpedia
citations.quote: negotiated a land deal with South Carolina that established clear title to a reservation 15 miles square

claims.notes: NCpedia dates the land deal with South Carolina to 1759; the South Carolina Encyclopedia dates the confirming grant to the 1763 Treaty of Augusta. By the early 1800s almost all of the reservation had been leased to settlers (SCE).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Nation Ford (March 1840) the Catawba agreed to give up their lands in exchange for a government pledge of $5,000 to buy land elsewhere; the treaty was made with the state of South Carolina.

citations.title: Catawba People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Catawba agreed to give up their lands in exchange for a government pledge to spend $5,000 to purchase land for them elsewhere.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In 1840 the Catawba Nation and the state of South Carolina entered into the Treaty of Nation Ford

citations.title: Catawba people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1840, by the Treaty of Nation Ford with South Carolina, the Catawba sold to the state all but one square mile

citations.title: Catawba people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The treaty was invalid ab initio because the state did not have the right to make it

claims.notes: Sources differ on the replacement land (300 acres in North Carolina, SCE; none, NCpedia) and on whether any land was retained. The Catawba returned to the ceded land and the state withheld payments (SCE). Wikipedia says the treaty was invalid ab initio (no Congressional approval).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: A tract of 630 acres near the centre of the old reservation was secured for the Catawba in 1843; the Catawba Indian Nation, federally recognized again in 1993, is headquartered at Rock Hill.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Joseph White in 1843 to secure for them a tract of 630 acres near the center of the "Old Reservation."

citations.title: Catawba people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1993 they regained federal recognition and won a $50 million Indian land claims settlement

claims.notes: The Catawba were federally recognized in 1941, terminated in 1959, and regained recognition in 1993.

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

claims.statement: The Tuscarora occupied the inner Coastal Plain of North Carolina; their Lower Towns, on the lower Neuse River and Contentnea Creek under Chief Hancock, fought the war of 1711-13, and Fort Neoheroka (Greene County) fell in March 1713.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Tuscarora American Indian people occupied much of the North Carolina inner Coastal Plain at the time of the Roanoke Island colonies in the 1580s.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Lower Towns, on the lower Neuse River and the Catechna (now Contentnea) Creek, led by Chief Hancock

claims.notes: Start is "circa" (1580s). Upper Towns lay on the upper Neuse, Tar and Roanoke rivers (NCpedia). Place = Fort Neoheroka (Greene County) standing for the Lower Towns; the Upper Towns lay further inland.

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

claims.statement: After the defeat at Fort Neoheroka (20-23 March 1713) the Tuscarora who had fought the colonists left North Carolina, migrating north over many years and joining the Five Nations (Haudenosaunee), who accepted them as the sixth nation in 1722.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Tuscaroras who had opposed the settlers removed to Niagara County, N.Y., to join the Five Nations, thereafter the Six Nations.

citations.title: Tuscarora people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1722, sponsored by the Oneida, the Tuscarora were accepted as the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

claims.notes: Date is approximate: the northward migration took place over about 90 years (Wikipedia) and the Haudenosaunee admission is dated 1722.

place.name: Indian Woods Reservation, Bertie County, North Carolina

claims.statement: Tom Blount's Upper Town Tuscarora, who had aided the colonists, were given a reservation (Indian Woods) on the Roanoke River in Bertie County, North Carolina, in 1717.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: Lands on the north side of the Roanoke River between Quitsna Swamp and Deep Creek in southwestern Bertie County were secured in 1717

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: were rewarded with a reservation

claims.notes: Coordinates are the Bertie County point (approximate). End year 1831 is the deed extinguishing Tuscarora title.

place.name: Indian Woods Reservation, Bertie County, North Carolina

claims.statement: In 1831 the Tuscarora executed a deed to North Carolina extinguishing their title and interest in the Indian Woods lands.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: the Tuscarora executed a deed to the state in 1831 extinguishing their title, right, and interest in the North Carolina land

claims.notes: About 645 families remained in the South and later re-formed communities in and around Robeson County; four Tuscarora communities there were not officially recognized by North Carolina as of the early 2000s (NCpedia).

place.name: Pocotaligo (Yamasee town), near Yemassee, South Carolina

claims.statement: The Yamasee settled near the Savannah River in the 1680s and built towns including Pocotaligo, the main Upper Yamasee town, in what is now Beaufort County, South Carolina.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: They established several villages, including Pocotaligo, Tolemato, and Topiqui, in Beaufort County.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Yamasee became prominent in the history of South Carolina when they settled near the Savannah River in the 1680s.

citations.title: Yamasee War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the main Upper Yamasee town of Pocotaligo

claims.notes: Start is approximate: Wikipedia places the move in 1687 and "the 1680s". Coordinates are the community of Pocotaligo, SC (approximate; near Yemassee).

place.name: Pocotaligo (Yamasee town), near Yemassee, South Carolina

claims.statement: After the Yamasee War began in April 1715 and the Yamasee were defeated, they were driven from South Carolina across the Savannah River into Spanish Florida; by spring 1716 most had settled in Florida.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Eventually, Craven was able to drive the Yamasees across the Savannah River back into Spanish Florida.

citations.title: Yamassee War - NCpedia
citations.quote: By the spring of 1716, most of the Yamassee had settled in Florida.

claims.notes: Place = the Yamasee towns around Pocotaligo they were driven from.

claims.statement: After the war many Yamasee settled in the region around St. Augustine and Pensacola in Spanish Florida; some remained near St. Augustine until Spain gave up the city to Britain in 1763.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: After the war, the Yamasees migrated southwards to the region around St. Augustine and Pensacola, where they formed an alliance with the Spanish colonial administration.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Still others remained near St. Augustine until the Spanish relinquished control of the city to the British in 1763.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only; smallpox and raids in 1727 led many Yamasee to disperse, some joining the Seminole or Creek, and about 90 evacuated to Havana in 1763.

place.name: Anhaica / Mission San Luis de Apalachee, Tallahassee, Florida

claims.statement: The Apalachee lived in Apalachee Province in the Florida Panhandle, one of the most powerful and wealthy chiefdoms in Florida, whose capital Anhaica lay at present Tallahassee, later the site of Spain's Mission San Luis.

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Apalachee Province was one of the most powerful and wealthy chiefdoms or provinces in Florida

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: capital of Apalachee Province

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1528, Pánfilo de Narváez is the first recorded European presence in Apalachee

claims.notes: Start year is the first European record (Narváez, 1528); Apalachee lived there long before. De Soto wintered at Anhaica in 1539-40.

place.name: Anhaica / Mission San Luis de Apalachee, Tallahassee, Florida

claims.statement: In January 1704 Carolina colonists under James Moore and their Muscogee allies raided the Apalachee missions; Mission San Luis was evacuated and destroyed that year, and most Apalachee were killed, captured, fled, or resettled near the Savannah and Ocmulgee rivers.

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The mission lasted until 1704 when it was evacuated and destroyed to prevent its use by an approaching militia of Creek Indians and South Carolinians.

citations.title: Apalachee massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: most of their population were either killed, captured, fled to larger Spanish and French outposts, or voluntarily joined the English

citations.title: Apalachee massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: They were resettled near the Savannah and Ocmulgee Rivers, where living conditions proved to be only slightly better.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only. The Apalachee population in 1680 was about 8,000 across 14 missions.

place.name: Fort Caroline area (Saturiwa Timucua), St. Johns River, Florida

claims.statement: The Timucua, independent chiefdoms of northeast Florida, included the Saturiwa near the St. Johns River at present Jacksonville, where the French built Fort Caroline in 1564; slave raids and disease reduced the Timucua to about 1,000 people by 1700.

citations.title: Timucua - Wikipedia
citations.quote: European contact with the Eastern Timucua began in 1564 when the French Huguenots under René Goulaine de Laudonnière established Fort Caroline in Saturiwa territory.

citations.title: Timucua - Wikipedia
citations.quote: By 1700, the population of the tribe had been reduced to an estimated 1,000 due to slave raids from Carolinian settlers and their Indian allies.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only; start year is the first documented French contact with the Saturiwa, not the beginning of Timucua presence (earlier Spanish contact 1513-1528). The Timucua were never a single political unit.

place.name: Fort Caroline area (Saturiwa Timucua), St. Johns River, Florida

claims.statement: When Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 the Spanish took the fewer than 100 surviving Timucua and other native people to Cuba.

citations.title: Timucua - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1763, when Spain ceded Florida to Great Britain, the Spanish took the less than 100 Timucua and other natives to Cuba.

claims.notes: The source does not name the Timucua departure point; the Fort Caroline area is used only as a Timucua anchor. Research on possible Timucua descendants in Cuba is under way (Wikipedia).

place.name: Mound Key (Calos, Calusa capital), Estero Bay, Florida

claims.statement: The Calusa kingdom of southwest Florida was ruled from its capital Calos, probably at Mound Key in Estero Bay, when the Spanish first explored the coast in the early 1500s.

citations.title: Calusa - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The capital of the Calusa, and from where the rulers administered, was Mound Key, near present day Estero, Florida.

citations.title: Mound Key Archaeological State Park - Florida State Parks
citations.quote: Mound Key is believed to have been the ceremonial center of the Calusa Indians when the Spaniards first explored Southwest Florida in the early 1500s.

claims.notes: Start year is the 1566 eyewitness account of the king's house; the Calusa had held the coast for over 2,000 years (Florida State Parks). End year is the final removal to Cuba in 1763; survivors had already left their capital earlier under disease and slave raids.

place.name: Mound Key (Calos, Calusa capital), Estero Bay, Florida

claims.statement: In 1711 the Spanish evacuated about 270 people, including many Calusa, from the Florida Keys to Cuba, and after Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 the Spanish relocated the remaining south Florida peoples to Cuba, completing their removal.

citations.title: Calusa - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the remaining tribes of South Florida were relocated to Cuba by the Spanish, completing their removal from the region

citations.title: Calusa - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1711, the Spanish helped evacuate 270 Indians, including many Calusa, from the Florida Keys to Cuba

claims.notes: Wikipedia only for the removal; place = the Calusa capital.

place.name: Coosa capital (Little Egypt site), Coosawattee River area, Murray County, Georgia

claims.statement: The Coosa paramount chiefdom, centred on the Coosawattee River in northwest Georgia (the "Little Egypt" site), dominated several smaller chiefdoms and was inhabited from at least 1400 until about 1600, when most of its core area was abandoned.

citations.title: Coosa chiefdom - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It was inhabited from at least 1400 until about 1600 CE, and dominated several smaller chiefdoms.

citations.title: Coosa chiefdom - Wikipedia
citations.quote: By the close of the 16th century, most of the core area of the Coosa was abandoned.

citations.title: Cherokee Indians - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: With the arrival of Spanish explorers and Old World diseases, the chiefdoms collapsed

claims.notes: Dates approximate. Coordinates are Murray County, Georgia (approximate; the capital site is on the Coosawattee River in Gordon/Murray counties). Coosa is also the name of one of the four Muscogee mother towns.

claims.statement: Cahokia, a Mississippian city near present St. Louis, existed from about 1050 to 1350 and may have had 10,000-20,000 people at its peak between 1050 and 1150.

citations.title: Cahokia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: is the site of a Native American city which existed c. 1050 - c. 1350 AD

citations.title: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
citations.quote: This agricultural society may have had a population of 10-20,000 at its peak between 1050 and 1150.

claims.notes: Pre-1492 background. UNESCO dates occupation to the Mississippian period (800-1400). The later Cahokia tribe (Illiniwek) was not necessarily descended from the earlier inhabitants (Wikipedia).

claims.statement: Moundville on the Black Warrior River in Alabama was founded around 1120 and gradually ceased to be a town between 1300 and 1450 as its mounds fell out of use and most inhabitants left.

citations.title: Moundville Archaeological Park - Encyclopedia of Alabama
citations.quote: The Moundville site was founded around 1120 by Native American peoples of the Mississippian period

citations.title: Moundville Archaeological Park - Encyclopedia of Alabama
citations.quote: Between 1300 and 1450, the mounds gradually fell out of use, and most of Moundville's inhabitants left the great town.

claims.notes: Pre-1492 background. The Encyclopedia of Alabama says the site was abandoned in the sixteenth century.

claims.statement: Etowah, on the Etowah River near present Cartersville, Georgia, was a Mississippian mound town settled by the twelfth century (perhaps two centuries earlier) and occupied, with brief abandonments, into the seventeenth century.

citations.title: Etowah Mounds - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The town was settled by the twelfth century; many archaeologists date the settlement at least two centuries earlier.

citations.title: Etowah Mounds - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Its occupation continued, with brief periods of abandonment, into the seventeenth century.

claims.notes: Pre-1492 background. Dates approximate; occupation was intermittent.

place.name: Mabila (site uncertain; Marengo County, Alabama region)

claims.statement: Mabila was a fortified town of the paramount chief Tuskaloosa in central Alabama; in October 1540 it was the scene of a major battle with de Soto's Spanish expedition, in which the town was burned.

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: was a small fortress town under a polity led by Tuskaloosa in 1540, in a region of present-day central Alabama

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On October 18, 1540, de Soto and the expedition arrived at Mabila, a heavily fortified village situated on a plain.

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Armed with guns, the Spaniards eventually burned down the village and killed most of the warriors.

claims.notes: The exact location of Mabila is unknown; coordinates are the centre of Marengo County, Alabama, where 2021 archaeology located the province of Mabila (approximate).

place.name: xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam), mouth of the Fraser River

claims.statement: The Musqueam (xʷməθkʷəy̓əm), a hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓-speaking Coast Salish people, have lived and moved through their territory at the mouth of the Fraser River (Point Grey, Vancouver) for thousands of years and remain there on the Musqueam Indian Reserve.

citations.title: Musqueam's Story - Musqueam Indian Band
citations.quote: We have always moved throughout our territory using the resources it provides for fishing, hunting, trapping and gathering

citations.title: Musqueam Indian Band - Wikipedia
citations.quote: have lived in the Point Grey area (today part of Vancouver), around the mouth of the Fraser River, for at least 4,000 years

claims.notes: from=1492 is the start of the map window, NOT a founding date: sources describe occupation since time immemorial / long before 1492. the source states continuous presence for thousands of years. Coordinate is the Wikidata point for Musqueam First Nation (reserve), not a single village.

place.name: Burrard Inlet and Howe Sound (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw, Squamish Nation)

claims.statement: The Squamish (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh) have lived across Howe Sound and Burrard Inlet for thousands of years; reserves there were allotted and surveyed at village and food-gathering sites between 1876 and 1888.

citations.title: Our History - Squamish Nation
citations.quote: Our rich history spans millennia, evidenced by an archaeological site dating back 8,600 years

citations.title: Our History - Squamish Nation
citations.quote: 1876 - 1888 Creation of Reserves Reserve lands along Howe Sound and Burrard Inlet were allotted and surveyed

claims.notes: from=1492 is the start of the map window, NOT a founding date: sources describe occupation since time immemorial / long before 1492. the source states continuous presence for thousands of years. The 1876-1888 reserve allotment left 'all remaining land' claimed as Crown land per the Nation's own timeline; there was no treaty.

claims.statement: In April 1850 James Douglas met leaders of the Lekwungen (now the Songhees and Esquimalt First Nations) and made verbal agreements, the first of the fourteen land purchases known as the Douglas Treaties (1850-1854) on Vancouver Island.

citations.title: Douglas Treaties - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Douglas met first in April 1850 with leaders of the Lekwungen people (now Songhees and Esquimalt First Nations), and made verbal agreements

citations.title: Douglas Treaties - Wikipedia
citations.quote: made a series of fourteen land purchases from First Nations

claims.notes: Wikipedia only; the later written terms of the treaty were recorded separately from the verbal agreement. Whether the First Nations understood the transactions as cessions of title is disputed in the literature.

place.name: Medicine Creek treaty lands (Nisqually delta to Mount Rainier)

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Medicine Creek (26 December 1854) the Nisqually, Puyallup, Steilacoom, Squaxin Island and related bands ceded some 2.5 million acres of south Puget Sound, keeping three small reservations and fishing and hunting rights.

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: cede nearly all their lands, retaining three tiny reservations and access to traditional hunting and fishing grounds

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: encompassed some 2.5 million acres extending from south Puget Sound to the slopes of Mount Rainier

claims.notes: Coordinate is the Nisqually Reservation point (Wikidata) as a stand-in for the treaty ground on the Nisqually delta.

claims.statement: After the armed conflict that followed the 1854-55 treaties, in August 1856 Governor Isaac Stevens agreed with Puyallup and Nisqually leaders to significantly larger reservations for both tribes than the treaty had provided.

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: in August 1856 Stevens will meet with Puyallup and Nisqually leaders and agree to significantly larger reservations for both tribes

citations.title: Puyallup Tribe of Indians - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the reservation was established in 1854 in the Treaty of Medicine Creek

claims.notes: Homeland-on-reservation claim from the 1856 enlargement; the Puyallup lived on the Puyallup River long before.

place.name: Lummi Reservation (Lummi Peninsula, mouth of the Nooksack River)

claims.statement: The Lummi (Xwlemi; Lhaq'temish) were party to the Treaty of Point Elliott in January 1855, which established the Lummi Reservation near the mouth of the Nooksack River on the Lummi Peninsula.

citations.title: Lummi Nation - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the 12,562.94 acre Lummi Reservation was established near the mouth of the Nooksack River, on the Lummi Peninsula

citations.title: Treaty of Point Elliott - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The treaty established the Suquamish Port Madison, Tulalip, Swin-a-mish (Swinomish), and Lummi reservations

claims.notes: Wikipedia only. Coordinate is the Nooksack River point from Wikidata (approximate stand-in for the reservation). Before 1855 the Lummi occupied settlements across the San Juan Islands and mainland per Wikipedia.

place.name: Duwamish River and Elliott Bay villages (Seattle)

claims.statement: The Duwamish (dxʷdəwʔabš) lived in at least 17 villages near Elliott Bay, the Duwamish and Black rivers, Lake Washington and Lake Sammamish, with the center of their society around the Black and Duwamish rivers.

citations.title: Duwamish Tribe wins federal recognition on January 19, 2001 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: The Duwamish Tribe occupied at least 17 villages near Elliott Bay, Duwamish River, Black River (which no longer exists), Lake Washington, and Lake Sammamish

citations.title: Duwamish people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Prior to colonization, the center of Duwamish society was around the Black and Duwamish rivers in Washington

claims.notes: from=1492 is the start of the map window, NOT a founding date: sources describe occupation since time immemorial / long before 1492. the source states continuous presence for thousands of years. 'to' 1855 is the Treaty of Point Elliott cession date; Duwamish people continued to live in the area (see contested claim).

place.name: Point Elliott treaty cession (Duwamish lands, Seattle)

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Point Elliott (22 January 1855) the Duwamish, with Chief Seattle (Si'ahl) and other signers, ceded their lands to the United States in exchange for cash, reservations and reserved fishing and hunting rights.

citations.title: Chief Seattle and other Puget Sound leaders sign Point Elliott Treaty on January 22, 1855 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: Tribes including the Duwamish and Suquamish surrender their lands for cash, relocation to reservations, and access to traditional fishing and hunting grounds

citations.title: Duwamish Tribe wins federal recognition on January 19, 2001 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: The Duwamish, including Chief Seattle (178?-1866), for whom Seattle is named, were among the signers of the Point Elliott treaty, signed on January 22, 1855

claims.notes: Treaty ratified by the US Senate in 1859 (HistoryLink 2951 and Suquamish Tribe page).

place.name: Black River-Cedar River confluence (Renton), Duwamish homeland

claims.statement: Yaanga, the largest and most influential Tongva village in the Los Angeles Basin, stood near present downtown Los Angeles; the Tongva homeland covered Los Angeles County and the southern Channel Islands.

citations.title: Yaanga - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Yaanga was a large Tongva (or Kizh) village, originally located near what is now downtown Los Angeles

citations.title: Gabrielino/Tongva Nation
citations.quote: Our traditional homelands encompassed Los Angeles County and the islands of Santa Catalina, San Nicholas, San Clemente, and Santa Barbara

claims.notes: The village survived the pueblo founding of 1781 as a "refugee camp" before being dispersed (see next claim).

claims.statement: After the founding of the Pueblo de Los Ángeles in 1781 Yaanga was forcibly relocated several times and was finally razed to the ground by the Los Angeles City Council under American occupation in 1847.

citations.title: Yaanga - Wikipedia
citations.quote: it was razed to the ground by the Los Angeles City Council under American occupation in 1847

claims.notes: Wikipedia-only for this detail. Wikipedia also says the original village stayed intact only until about 1813.

claims.statement: Mission San Gabriel was founded among the Tongva in 1771 after the 1769 Portolá expedition; under the mission system the Spanish forced the relocation and virtual enslavement of the people to secure their labor.

citations.title: Gabrielino/Tongva Nation
citations.quote: we are more widely known by our connection to the San Gabriel Mission beginning in 1771

citations.title: Tongva - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Under the mission system, the Spanish initiated an era of forced relocation and virtual enslavement of the peoples to secure their labor.

claims.notes: The sources read give only the year 1771.

place.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá (Kumeyaay Nipawai), California

claims.statement: The site of Mission San Diego, the Kumeyaay village of Nipawai in the San Diego River valley, lay in an area long inhabited by the Kumeyaay (Tiipay) people.

citations.title: Mission San Diego de Alcalá - Wikipedia
citations.quote: in an area long inhabited by the Kumeyaay people

citations.title: San Diego de Alcalá - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: The native Tipai-Ipai Indians were resistant to colonization

claims.notes: The Kumeyaay remained in the region; "to" marks the Spanish mission founding on their land. Kumeyaay are not on the shared registry and are added here.

place.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá (Kumeyaay Nipawai), California

claims.statement: Within weeks of the founding of Mission San Diego on 16 July 1769 violence caused deaths on both sides; in 1775 hundreds of Tipai attacked and burned the mission and killed Father Luis Jayme.

citations.title: San Diego de Alcalá - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: Founded by Father Junipero Serra on July 16, 1769

citations.title: San Diego de Alcalá - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: hundreds of local Tipai Indians attacked the mission, causing great damage to the building and killing Father Jayme

claims.notes: The day of the 1775 revolt (traditionally 4-5 November) is not given in the sources read.

place.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá (Kumeyaay Nipawai), California

claims.statement: After Mexican independence Mexican troops confiscated all coastal lands from the Kumeyaay in 1822 and granted them to Californio settlers, beginning the rancho era.

citations.title: Kumeyaay - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Mexican troops confiscated all coastal lands from the Kumeyaay in 1822

claims.notes: Wikipedia-only. Seizure, not a treaty; coastal lands only.

place.name: Clear Lake, Lake County (Bloody Island), California

claims.statement: Pomo territory extended from the Pacific coast inland to Clear Lake; the island at the north end of the lake (Bo-no-po-ti, "Island Village") was a traditional gathering place for the spring fish spawn.

citations.title: Pomo - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Historical Pomo territory in Northern California was large, bordered by the Pacific Coast to the west, extending inland to Clear Lake

citations.title: Bloody Island massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It was a place where the Pomo had traditionally gathered for the spring fish spawn.

claims.notes: The Pomo were many independent tribelets and bands; Clear Lake is an anchor. Wikipedia-only.

claims.statement: The Kashaya Pomo lived on the coastline near Fort Ross, where Russian colonists settled from 1812 to 1841 and traded with them.

citations.title: Pomo - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Pomo who lived on the coastline and near Fort Ross were known as the Kashaya.

claims.notes: Wikipedia-only.

claims.statement: The Ahwahnechee (Awani), a band of Mono and Miwok people, lived in Yosemite Valley for centuries, possibly 7,000 years, until the Mariposa Battalion entered the valley in 1851.

citations.title: Ahwahnechee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Awani lived in Yosemite Valley for centuries.

citations.title: Ahwahnechee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It is believed that they may have lived in the area for as long as 7,000 years.

claims.notes: Wikipedia describes the Ahwahnechee as a band of Mono and Miwok; Miwok groups (Plains, Sierra, Coast, Lake) held much of the Sierra foothills and Sacramento Valley.

claims.statement: On 25 March 1851 the California Militia's Mariposa Battalion entered Yosemite Valley, burned Ahwahnechee villages and food stores and forcibly relocated people from the valley; Chief Tenaya was captured and his band surrendered.

citations.title: Mariposa Battalion - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the battalion entered the Yosemite Valley and burned Native American villages and food supplies and forcibly relocated people from their homes in the valley

citations.title: Ahwahnechee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: This was the first entry into Yosemite Valley by any white men.

claims.notes: Wikipedia dates the first entry to 25 March 1851; other histories give 27 March. Some Ahwahnechee returned to the valley later.

claims.statement: Round Valley was the land of the Yuki people before the reservation system; the Round Valley Indian Tribes now include the Yuki, Wailaki, Concow Maidu, Little Lake and other Pomo, Nomlaki and Pit River peoples.

citations.title: Round Valley Indian Reservation - Wikipedia
citations.quote: to land originally occupied by the Yuki people in Round Valley

citations.title: Round Valley Indian Reservation - Wikipedia
citations.quote: These include the Yuki, Wailaki, Concow (or Konkow), Little Lake and other Pomo, Nomlaki, and Pit River peoples.

claims.notes: To = 1856, when the Nome Cult Farm was begun in Round Valley.

claims.statement: From 1856 other California peoples, including Concow Maidu marched about 100 miles from the Sacramento Valley (the Nome Cult Trail), were forced onto the Nome Cult Farm and Round Valley Reservation in Yuki country, where massacres between 1858 and 1860 killed more than 500 people.

citations.title: Round Valley Indian Reservation - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Round Valley Indian Reservation began in 1856 as the Nome Cult Farm

citations.title: Round Valley Indian Reservation - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The 100 mile march became known as the Concow Trail of Tears or the Nome Cult Trail.

citations.title: California genocide - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Massacres in Round Valley between 1858 and 1860 killed more than 500 people.

claims.notes: Place is the destination; the Concow removal date is not given in the sources read.

claims.statement: President Grant formally established the Round Valley Indian Reservation by Executive Order on 30 March 1870; it is now home to the Round Valley Indian Tribes, a sovereign confederation of tribes.

citations.title: Round Valley Indian Reservation - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Grant formally established the Round Valley Indian Reservation by Executive Order on March 30, 1870

citations.title: Round Valley Indian Tribes
citations.quote: A Sovereign Nation of Confederated Tribes

place.name: Ishi Wilderness / Mill Creek country (Yahi homeland), California

claims.statement: The Yana were based between the Pit and Feather rivers in northeastern California, with the Yahi in the southern portion, a people who fiercely defended their mountain canyons; after the 1865 Three Knolls Massacre and years of killings the Yahi were destroyed, and Ishi, the last Yahi, emerged near Oroville in 1911.

citations.title: Ishi - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Ishi Wilderness Area in northeastern California, believed to be the ancestral grounds of his tribe, is named in his honor.

citations.title: Ishi - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1865, the Yahi were attacked in the Three Knolls Massacre, in which 40 of them were killed.

claims.notes: Wikipedia-only. Yana peoples (Central and Southern Yana) survive as members of Redding Rancheria.

events.title: Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan formed
events.statement: After defeating Azcapotzalco in 1428, Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan formed the Triple Alliance that dominated the Valley of Mexico until 1521.

citations.title: Aztec Triple Alliance (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1427, Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan, and Huexotzinco went to war against Azcapotzalco, emerging victorious in 1428.

citations.title: Aztec Civilization (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: 1428 The Triple Alliance is formed between Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan.

events.notes: Wikipedia notes that the three remaining cities formalised their treaty in 1430 after the 1428 victory.

events.title: Tlaxcallan allies with Cortés
events.statement: After fighting the Spanish army in late August 1519, the Tlaxcalan lords received Cortés in their capital on 18 September 1519 and agreed to provide provisions and warriors against the Mexica.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: On August 31, at a point ten miles into Tlaxcalan territory, Cortés' army encountered a hostile force of at least 30,000 Tlaxcalans.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Xicotenga agreed to provide necessary provisions and manpower to the Spaniards.

citations.title: Tlaxcallan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Due to protracted warfare between the Aztecs and the Tlaxcalteca, the latter were eager to exact revenge, and soon became loyal allies of the Spanish.

events.notes: 18 September is the date the army entered the capital per Schmal; the alliance was negotiated over the following twenty days.

events.title: La Noche Triste: Spanish and Tlaxcalan forces driven from Tenochtitlan
events.statement: Cortés's army and its Tlaxcalan and other native allies were driven out of Tenochtitlan by the Mexica, leaving at night along the western causeway toward Tlacopan.

citations.title: Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: including their native allies were driven out of the Mexica capital, Tenochtitlan.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: 30 June - "La Noche Triste" - Evacuation of Spanish-Tlaxcalteca allied forces from Tenochtitlan

citations.title: Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On the night of July 1, 1520, Cortez's large army left their compound and headed west, toward the Tlacopan causeway.

events.notes: Date conflict: the conquest timeline gives 30 June; the Noche Triste article says the army left on the night of 1 July 1520. 30 June used.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic in the Valley of Mexico
events.statement: Smallpox spread to Tepeaca and Tlaxcala and reached Tenochtitlan by the fall of 1520, killing native rulers including Cuitláhuac and, by one estimate, a quarter to a half of the population of central Mexico.

citations.title: History of smallpox in Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: From May to September, smallpox spread slowly to Tepeaca and Tlaxcala, and to Tenochtitlán by the fall of 1520.

citations.title: History of smallpox in Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: However, Cuitláhuac and other native rulers also died of smallpox.

citations.title: History of smallpox in Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Estimates of mortality range from one-quarter to one-half of the population of central Mexico.

citations.title: Smallpox Kills Thousands of Indigenous Americans (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: it contributed to the collapse of Aztec resistance against the Spanish, facilitating Cortés's conquest of Tenochtitlán by 1521.

events.notes: Wikipedia's conquest timeline dates the epidemic in the capital to mid-October to mid-December 1520, with Cuitláhuac dying on 4 December 'perhaps of smallpox'.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
events.statement: After a siege beginning in 1521, Tenochtitlan surrendered to Cortés and his Tlaxcalan and other native allies on 13 August 1521, ending the Mexica empire.

citations.title: Tenochtitlan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On the 13th of August 1521, after over two months of fighting, Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés succeeded in bringing about the fall of Tenochtitlan

citations.title: Tenochtitlan (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: he was able to lay siege to the city which would eventually fall on the 13th of August 1521 CE.

events.title: Tangaxuan II executed; end of Purépecha independence
events.statement: Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán had the last Cazonci, Tangaxuan II, executed on 14 February 1530; the Purépecha state lost its independence to the Spanish in 1530.

citations.title: Tangaxuan II (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: He was executed by burning by Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán on February 14, 1530.

citations.title: Purépecha Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The kingdom was founded in the early 14th century and lost its independence to the Spanish in 1530.

events.notes: Place is the Purépecha capital; the sources do not give where the execution took place. Event kind is a political killing, not a mass removal.

events.title: Mixtón War begins
events.statement: In 1540 the Caxcanes and allies rose against Spanish rule in Nueva Galicia; the war centred on the hill of Mixtón and ended in defeat in 1542.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Mixtón War (1540-1542) was an uprising by Caxcan people aimed at pushing the Spanish conquistadors out of northwestern Mexico

citations.title: The Caxcanes of Nochistlán: Defenders of Their Homeland (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Tenamaxtle, originally from Nochistlan, was one of the leaders of this rebellion which quickly spread south.

events.notes: Place is Nochistlán, the home of Tenamaztle; the Mixtón hill is in Zacatecas. Some accounts date the war 1540-1541.

events.title: Xiu lord of Maní allies with the Spanish at Mérida
events.statement: After the Spanish founded Mérida at T'ho on 6 January 1542, the Tutul-Xiu lord of Maní came in peace on 23 January; the Xiu's friendship and conversion encouraged other western provinces to accept Spanish rule.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On 23 January, Tutul-Xiu, the lord of Maní, approached the Spanish encampment at Mérida in peace, bearing sorely needed food supplies.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: his submission to Spain and conversion to Christianity encouraged the lords of the western provinces to accept Spanish rule.

events.title: Cocoliztli epidemic of 1545-1548
events.statement: The cocoliztli epidemic of 1545-1548 killed an estimated five to fifteen million people, about 800,000 of them in the Valley of Mexico; a contact-era cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca is the only one conclusively linked to its victims, and a second large outbreak followed in 1576.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: At least 12 epidemics are attributed to cocoliztli, with the largest occurring in 1545, 1576, 1736, and 1813.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Around 800,000 died in the Valley of Mexico

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Estimates for the entire number of human lives lost during this epidemic have ranged from 5 to 15 million people

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Contact-era site has the only cemetery to be conclusively linked to victims of the outbreak of 1545-1548.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A second large outbreak of cocoliztli occurred in 1576, lasting until about 1580.

events.notes: Place is the Valley of Mexico (Tenochtitlan site); the epidemic was widespread. The cause is debated (paratyphoid or a viral hemorrhagic fever). Death-toll estimates vary widely; Wikipedia gives 5-15 million. The 1576 epidemic is a separate outbreak, not separately dated here.

events.title: Chichimeca War begins
events.statement: Following the 1546 silver strike at Zacatecas, Zacatecos attacked supply routes in late 1550 and the Guachichiles and Guamares joined in 1551, beginning the Chichimeca War, recorded as the longest and most expensive Spanish campaign against Indigenous people in the region.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The first outbreak of hostilities was in late 1550 when Zacatecos attacked supply routes of Purépecha.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1551 the Guachichile and Guamares joined in

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Chichimeca War is recorded as both the longest and most expensive military campaign confronting the Spanish Empire and indigenous people in Aridoamerica.

events.notes: End date varies by source (1590 or 1600).

events.title: Tepehuán Revolt
events.statement: On 16 November 1616 a wagon train was attacked near Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes, beginning the Tepehuán Revolt against Spanish settlements and missions; it was officially declared at an end in 1620.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 16, 1616, a wagon train traveling to Mexico City was attacked by the Tepehuán just outside Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes

citations.title: Servant of God Fr Hernando de Santaren & Companions, SJ (Jesuits Singapore)
citations.quote: when they were martyred by the Tepehuan Indians living in northwestern Mexico (today's Durango) between November 16 and 20, 1616.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The revolt was officially declared at an end in 1620

events.notes: The Jesuit page is a devotional source; it agrees on the November 1616 dates.

events.title: Rarámuri war of 1648 and destruction of San Francisco de Borja mission
events.statement: In 1648 the Rarámuri waged war on the Spanish, gathered at Fariagic and destroyed the mission of San Francisco de Borja; two leaders were captured and executed.

citations.title: Rarámuri (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1648, the Rarámuri waged war against the Spanish.

citations.title: Rarámuri (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They gathered at Fariagic and then destroyed the mission of San Francisco de Borja.

citations.title: Rarámuri (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Two of the leaders of this attack were captured by the Spanish and executed.

events.notes: A Spanish-language source cited in search results counts rebellions in 1648, 1652 and 1697; dates follow Wikipedia.

events.title: Fall of Nojpetén to the Spanish
events.statement: Martín de Ursúa's expedition took the island capital Nojpetén on 13 March 1697, the capital of the last Maya kingdom to fall to the Spanish, after the Itza king Kan Ek' did not accept conversion and surrender.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697

citations.title: Nojpetén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: it was the capital of the last Maya kingdom to fall to the conquerors.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Avendaño tried to convince Kan Ekʼ to convert to Christianity and surrender to the Spanish crown, without success.

citations.title: Chan Santa Cruz (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: General Martín de Ursúa invaded and sacked Nojpetén, the Itzá island capital, on March 13, 1697.

events.notes: Nojpetén article dates the assault to 10 March.

events.title: Caste War of Yucatán begins at Tepich
events.statement: Cecilio Chi and Jacinto Pat attacked Tepich on 30 July 1847, after the execution of the Maya leader Manuel Antonio Ay, opening the Caste War; the largest independent Maya state that emerged was named Chan Santa Cruz.

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cecilio Chi, the Maya leader of Tepich, with Jacinto Pat attacked Tepich on 30 July 1847.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: This act of retaliation is widely considered the official start of the Caste War of Yucatán.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: Manuel Antonio Ay was executed on July 26, 1847

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The largest of the independent Maya states was named Chan Santa Cruz, as was its capital city

events.notes: Start date varies: 30 June, 13 July and 30 July 1847 appear in different accounts; Wikipedia's Caste War article gives 30 July.

events.title: Fall of El Añil, the Yaqui fortress
events.statement: Mexican federal forces captured the main Yaqui fortress El Añil near Vícam on 12 May 1886 in the war against Cajemé's Yaqui republic.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: El Añil was captured on May 12, 1886.

citations.title: Yaqui (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: In 1886 almost four thousand Yaquis were captured during the Battle of Buatachive.

events.notes: Encyclopedia.com names this 1886 defeat the Battle of Buatachive; Wikipedia describes the capture of El Añil on 12 May 1886. Same campaign, different names.

events.title: Coronado's army takes Hawikuh (Cibola)
events.statement: In July 1540 Coronado's expedition fought some 600 Zuni warriors near Hawikuh and captured the town; some Zuni withdrew to Dowa Yalanne.

citations.title: Zuni people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Spanish met 600 Zuni warriors near Hawikuh in July 1540, inflicting several casualties, and capturing the village.

citations.title: Zuni (Encyclopedia of Native American Tribes via encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: In 1540 the Spanish entrada led by Francisco Vásquez de Coronado, came in search of gold to Zuni

events.title: Oñate's colony is founded at Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)
events.statement: In 1598 Juan de Oñate's colonising expedition entered the Pueblo country and made Ohkay Owingeh, which he renamed San Juan de los Caballeros, the seat of the new province of Santa Fe de Nuevo México.

citations.title: Juan de Oñate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: He held his colonial government at Ohkay Owingeh, and renamed the pueblo there 'San Juan de los Caballeros'.

citations.title: Acoma Pueblo (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: Juan de Oñate, who set out from Mexico in April, 1598, with a party of soldiers, their families, and a few Franciscans

events.notes: The expedition crossed the Rio Grande on 30 April 1598; the exact date the pueblo was occupied is not given in the sources used.

events.title: Acoma massacre
events.statement: In January 1599, after the killing of Juan de Zaldívar and some of his men at Acoma, Spanish forces under Vicente de Zaldívar stormed the mesa-top town; many were killed, about 500 were captured and sentenced to servitude, and Oñate ordered mutilation.

citations.title: 1599 Acoma massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Acoma Massacre was a punitive expedition by Spanish conquistadors at the Acoma Pueblo in January, 1599.

citations.title: Acoma Pueblo: Ancient City in the Sky (NPS)
citations.quote: Oñate himself demanded sentencing survivors to indentured servitude and bodily mutilation.

citations.title: Acoma Pueblo (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: came to Ácoma on January 11, 1599, intending vengeance

events.notes: Sources differ on the day Vicente de Zaldívar arrived (EBSCO: 11 January; Wikipedia: 21 January, with the main battle on 22 January), on the date of the original clash (October or December 1598), and on casualty figures, so month precision is used.

events.title: Pueblo Revolt
events.statement: On 10 August 1680, led by Popé of Ohkay Owingeh, the Pueblo peoples rose together against Spanish rule, besieged Santa Fe and forced the colonists to retreat to El Paso; the Spanish did not return for twelve years.

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On August 10, the Puebloans rose up, stole the Spaniards' horses to prevent them from fleeing

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: On August 10, 1680, the uprising began unexpectedly

events.notes: Popé had planned the rising for 11 August and advanced it a day after the plot was discovered (Wikipedia); EBSCO says informants expected 13 August. The Hopi villages, which had not received the change, rose on the original schedule.

events.title: Vargas retakes Santa Fe
events.statement: On 14 September 1692 Diego de Vargas, with about 60 soldiers and 100 native auxiliaries, proclaimed Spanish repossession of Santa Fe without a fight; the Pueblos' resistance continued until his violent recapture in December 1693 and a further revolt in 1696.

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On September 14, 1692, de Vargas proclaimed a formal act of repossession.

citations.title: Diego de Vargas (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: He is known for leading the reconquest of the territory in 1692 following the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.

events.notes: Wikipedia (Vargas) says he returned to Santa Fe in July 1692 with a small contingent; the Pueblo Revolt article dates the arrival to 13 September and the proclamation to 14 September.

events.title: Destruction of Awatovi
events.statement: In about 1700 Hopi villages that opposed Spanish missionary influence attacked Awatovi, where many had accepted Christianity, and destroyed the town, killing men and taking women and children captive; it has been a ruin since.

citations.title: Awatovi (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the end of 1700, the extreme hostility of most Hopis to Christian converts at Awatovi led to the destruction of the pueblo.

citations.title: Hopi (tribe) (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: the neighboring Hopi destroyed the village, killing the men and taking the women and children captive

events.notes: Sources give 'about the year 1700' / 'by the end of 1700'; the event was internal to the Hopi.

events.title: Taos Revolt
events.statement: On 19 January 1847, during the US conquest of New Mexico, Taos Pueblo people and Hispano neighbours rose against the new US territorial government at Taos.

citations.title: Taos Pueblo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On January 19, 1847, Hispanos and Taos Pueblo people launched a rebellion against the US territorial government.

events.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo

place.name: Villa de Guadalupe Hidalgo (Basilica of Guadalupe)

events.statement: Signed on 2 February 1848, the treaty transferred northern Mexico, including New Mexico and the lands of the Pueblo, Navajo, Apache, Ute and other nations, to the United States without their consent; Article XI committed the US to restrain Indian raids into Mexico.

citations.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was signed on the 2nd of February 1848 in the town of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

citations.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It provided that the United States would prevent and punish raids by Indians into Mexico

citations.title: Ute people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Following acquisition of Ute territory from Mexico by the Treaty of Guadalupe-Hidalgo 1848

events.notes: No Native nation of the Southwest was a party to the treaty.

events.title: Gadsden Purchase (Treaty of La Mesilla)
events.statement: In December 1853 the United States bought about 29,640 square miles of southern Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico, dividing the O'odham homeland between two countries; the nations living there were not parties to the sale.

citations.title: Gadsden Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The first draft was signed on December 31, 1853, by James Gadsden, US Minister to Mexico

citations.title: History & Culture - Tohono O'odham Nation (official site)
citations.quote: through the Gadsden Purchase or Treaty of La Mesilla, O'odham land was divided almost in half

events.notes: Wikipedia dates the first draft to 31 December 1853 (commonly given elsewhere as 30 December); month precision used.

events.title: Bascom affair
events.statement: In February 1861 Lt. George Bascom tried to hold Cochise and his family hostage at Apache Pass over the abduction of a boy from a ranch; Cochise cut his way out of the tent and a decade of war followed.

citations.title: Bascom affair (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Bascom attempted to imprison him and his family in a tent to be held hostage, but Cochise was able to escape alone

citations.title: The Battle of Apache Pass (NPS, Fort Bowie National Historic Site)
citations.quote: the memory of the Bascom Affair, that happened on this same ground just one year prior

events.notes: The original raid was by Tonto Apache, not Chiricahua (Wikipedia).

events.title: Battle of Apache Pass
events.statement: On 15-16 July 1862 Apache warriors (estimates range from about 150 to 500) under Cochise and Mangas Coloradas ambushed a California Column detachment at the springs in Apache Pass; the army then built Fort Bowie to hold the pass.

citations.title: Battle of Apache Pass (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: At noon on July 15, Roberts' detachment entered Apache Pass.

citations.title: The Battle of Apache Pass (NPS, Fort Bowie National Historic Site)
citations.quote: Cochise, who had recruited Mangas Coloradas

events.notes: NPS counts about 150 Apache warriors; Wikipedia says about 500. NPS dates the fight 15-16 July 1862.

events.title: Carson's campaign in Canyon de Chelly
events.statement: In January 1864 Col. Kit Carson's troops moved through Canyon de Chelly, destroying hogans, orchards and crops and seizing livestock; the resulting hunger and demoralisation led thousands of Diné to surrender and begin the Long Walk.

citations.title: Canyon de Chelly National Monument (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Kit Carson sent troops through the canyon, killing 23 Navajo, seizing 200 sheep, and destroying hogans

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Carson launched his full-scale assault on the Navajo population in January 1864.

events.title: The Long Walk to Bosque Redondo begins
events.statement: Beginning in March 1864 the US Army forced the Diné, in some 53 marches until the end of 1866, from their homeland to Bosque Redondo at Fort Sumner; thousands died in the marches and in internment.

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajos (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: the first, in March, 1864, was the largest

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Some 53 different forced marches occurred between August 1864 and the end of 1866.

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: up to 3,500 people died from starvation, disease and executions over a four-year period

events.notes: Estimates of those removed vary (about 8,500 to 10,000) and sources disagree on deaths (Wikipedia: up to 3,500).

events.title: Treaty of Bosque Redondo (Navajo Treaty of 1868)
events.statement: On 1 June 1868 Barboncito and other Diné headmen signed a treaty with Generals Sherman and Tappan at Fort Sumner that ended the Navajo Wars, created a Navajo reservation and allowed the people to return home.

citations.title: Treaty of Bosque Redondo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: an agreement between the Navajo and the US Federal Government signed on June 1, 1868

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajos (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: the Navajos' resilience eventually led to their return home in 1868 under a peace treaty

events.notes: Congress ratified the treaty on 25 July 1868 (per Wikipedia's Navajo Nation article).

events.title: Camp Grant massacre

place.name: Camp Grant massacre site (San Pedro River)

events.statement: On 30 April 1871 a force of Tucson settlers, Mexican Americans and Tohono O'odham from San Xavier attacked the Aravaipa and Pinal Apache refuge near Camp Grant, killing about 144, nearly all of them women and children.

citations.title: Camp Grant massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: All but eight of the corpses were women and children.

citations.title: Camp Grant massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Camp Grant massacre, on April 30, 1871, was an attack on Pinal and Aravaipa Apaches who surrendered to the United States Army

citations.title: Tohono O'odham (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: 92 O'odham joined 48 Mexicans and six Anglo-Americans and killed an estimated 144 Apache

events.notes: Wikipedia's Camp Grant article gives 144 Aravaipa and Pinal killed; the exact makeup of the attack force differs by source.

events.title: Brunot Agreement takes the San Juan Mountains from the Ute
events.statement: On 13 September 1873 at the Los Pinos Agency, Ute leaders signed the Brunot Agreement, ratified in 1874, under which Utes believed they were opening only part of the San Juan mountains to mining; they remember it as land taken by fraud.

citations.title: History - Southern Ute Indian Tribe (official site)
citations.quote: The Brunot Treaty was ratified by the United States in 1874

citations.title: History - Southern Ute Indian Tribe (official site)
citations.quote: most often remembered by Utes as the agreement when their land was fraudulently taken away

events.title: Meeker Massacre and Battle of Milk Creek (White River War)
events.statement: On 29 September 1879 White River Utes killed Indian agent Nathan Meeker and his male employees and ambushed an army column at Milk Creek, after Meeker's attempts to force farming and Christianity; the war led to the expulsion of the Utes from Colorado.

citations.title: Meeker Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Meeker Massacre, or Meeker Incident, White River War, Ute War, or the Ute Campaign), took place on September 29, 1879, in Colorado.

citations.title: Fifty for 150: Ute bands expelled from Colorado's Western Slope in 1881 (Colorado Newsline)
citations.quote: On Sept. 29, 1879, the Utes simultaneously ambushed the approaching Army unit and attacked the White River agency

events.title: Battle of Cibecue Creek
events.statement: In August 1881, after soldiers arrested the Cibecue Apache medicine man Nock-ay-det-klinne, fighting broke out at Cibecue Creek on the Fort Apache reservation and touched off a wider Apache uprising.

citations.title: Battle of Cibecue Creek (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Battle of Cibecue Creek was an engagement of the Apache Wars, fought in August 1881 between the United States and White Mountain Apaches

events.notes: Source gives August 1881 only.

events.title: Geronimo's final surrender at Skeleton Canyon
events.statement: On 4 September 1886 Geronimo and his small band of Chiricahua surrendered to General Nelson Miles at Skeleton Canyon, ending the Apache Wars; the whole Chiricahua people were then shipped to prison in Florida.

citations.title: Geronimo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: officially surrendered to General Miles on September 4, 1886, at Skeleton Canyon, Arizona

citations.title: Post Apache Wars (NPS, Chiricahua National Monument)
citations.quote: Geronimo's fourth and final surrender was in Skeleton Canyon in southern Arizona, the summer of 1886.

events.notes: Wikipedia says Geronimo surrendered three times; NPS counts four surrenders. Mescalero tribal page says he led 16 warriors, 12 women and six children at the surrender.

events.title: Quechan rising at the Yuma Crossing
events.statement: From 17 to 19 July 1781 the Quechan rose against the Spanish mission-settlements at the Yuma Crossing, destroyed them, and kept control of the crossing; the Spanish never again tried to control the Quechan or the crossing.

citations.title: Quechan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the tribe rebelled from July 17-19, 1781 and killed four priests and thirty soldiers

citations.title: Arizona: Yuma Crossing National Heritage Area (NPS)
citations.quote: After the Quechans destroyed the Spanish settlement at the crossing, the Spanish never again tried to control the Quechans or the Yuma Crossing.

events.title: Mohave War
events.statement: In 1858-1859 the Mohave fought the United States over emigrant traffic on the Beale Road and the Colorado crossing; the army built Fort Mojave in April 1859 and the Mohave accepted peace terms.

citations.title: Mohave War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Mohave War was an armed conflict between the Mohave people and the United States from 1858 to 1859.

citations.title: The People by the River - Fort Mojave Indian Tribe (official site)
citations.quote: Initially, this outpost was called Camp Colorado, but it was soon renamed Fort Mojave.

events.title: Battle of Cieneguilla
events.statement: On 30 March 1854 about 250 Jicarilla Apache and Ute fought US dragoons at Cieneguilla, near Pilar, during the Jicarilla War.

citations.title: Jicarilla Apache (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On March 30, 1854, a combined force of about 250 Apaches and Utes fought the U.S. dragoons

events.title: Fort Laramie (Horse Creek) Treaty of 1851

place.name: Mouth of Horse Creek, about 30 miles downriver from Fort Laramie (point shown is Fort Laramie)

events.statement: At a great council attended by thousands, United States commissioners and representatives of the Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow, Assiniboine, Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara signed a treaty on 17 September 1851 that defined each nation's territory and allowed roads and forts in exchange for annuities.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was signed on September 17, 1851 between United States treaty commissioners and representatives of the Cheyenne, Sioux, Arapaho, Crow, Assiniboine

citations.title: The Treaties of Fort Laramie, 1851 & 1868 (North Dakota Studies, State Historical Society of North Dakota)
citations.quote: The Treaty of 1851 did not establish a reservation, but began the process of defining territory in which the Sioux could live and hunt.

events.notes: Council held at Horse Creek; the treaty is also known as the Horse Creek Treaty. The Senate cut annuities from 50 to 10 years; the Crow did not accept the amendment.

events.title: Grattan fight (Grattan massacre)

place.name: Camp near Fort Laramie (east of the fort; point shown is Fort Laramie)

events.statement: On 19 August 1854 a US Army detachment under Lt. John Grattan entered a large Lakota camp east of Fort Laramie over a settler's cow; Chief Conquering Bear was mortally shot, the Brule Lakota returned fire and killed all 29 soldiers, beginning the First Sioux War.

citations.title: Grattan massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: occurring on August 19, 1854, between the United States Army and the Lakota Sioux warriors

citations.title: Grattan massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: resulting in the deaths of 29 soldiers, including Lieutenant John Grattan and a civilian interpreter

events.notes: Wikipedia only.

events.title: U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 begins
events.statement: With people starving and annuities late, four Dakota hunters killed five settlers at Acton on 17 August 1862; that night a council of Mdewakanton led by Taoyateduta (Little Crow) chose war, and the next day the Dakota attacked the Lower Sioux Agency, starting a six-week war in Minnesota.

citations.title: US-Dakota War of 1862 (MNopedia, Minnesota Historical Society)
citations.quote: On August 17, the tense situation reached a climax when four Dakota hunters killed five settlers in Acton Township.

citations.title: Dakota War of 1862 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On August 17, 1862, four young Dakota men killed five white settlers in Acton, Minnesota, after a disagreement.

events.notes: Fewer than 1,000 of more than 7,000 Dakota participated in the fighting (MNHS).

events.title: Mankato mass execution of 38 Dakota men
events.statement: On 26 December 1862 thirty-eight Dakota men were hanged together at Mankato, Minnesota, after military trials that sentenced 303 men to death; it was the largest one-day mass execution in American history.

citations.title: The Trials & Hanging (U.S.-Dakota War of 1862, Minnesota Historical Society)
citations.quote: On December 26, 1862, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato.

citations.title: US-Dakota War of 1862 (MNopedia, Minnesota Historical Society)
citations.quote: publicly executed thirty-eight Dakota men in Mankato at the largest mass hanging

citations.title: Dakota War of 1862 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: sentenced 303 Dakota men to death

events.notes: Kind marked as an execution (mass hanging).

events.title: Sand Creek massacre

place.name: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site

events.statement: On 29 November 1864 Colorado volunteers under Col. John Chivington attacked a camp of about 750 Cheyenne and Arapaho, led by Black Kettle, on Big Sandy Creek; most sources estimate about 150 people were killed, about two-thirds of them women and children.

citations.title: History & Culture (Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Chief Black Kettle settled his people, around 750 Cheyenne and Arapaho, in a bend of the Big Sandy Creek.

citations.title: Sand Creek massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: that occurred on November 29, 1864

citations.title: Sand Creek massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: most sources estimate around 150 people were killed, about two-thirds of whom were women and children

events.notes: Casualty estimates range from about 70 to over 600; most sources say about 150.

events.title: Fetterman Fight (Battle of the Hundred in the Hands)
events.statement: On 21 December 1866, during Red Cloud's War, Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors lured Captain William Fetterman's detachment from Fort Phil Kearny into an ambush and killed all 81 men, on land guaranteed to the Crow by treaty.

citations.title: Fetterman Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: during Red Cloud's War on December 21, 1866, between a confederation of the Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho tribes

citations.title: Fetterman Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: All 81 men under the command of Captain William J. Fetterman were then killed

events.notes: Wikipedia only. The Crow did not consent to the Lakota alliance operating on their treaty land.

events.title: Medicine Lodge treaties
events.statement: In October 1867 a US Indian Peace Commission signed three treaties at Medicine Lodge Creek, Kansas, with the Kiowa and Comanche, the Plains Apache, and the Cheyenne and Arapaho, relocating them to reservations in western Indian Territory; the Senate ratified them in July 1868.

citations.title: Medicine Lodge Treaty (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In October 1867 a U.S. Indian Peace Commission signed three treaties at Medicine Lodge Creek near Medicine Lodge, Kansas.

citations.title: Medicine Lodge Treaty (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The Senate ratified the treaties in July 1868.

events.notes: Article 12 required three-fourths of adult male approval for cessions, later at issue in Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock.

events.title: Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 (Great Sioux Reservation)
events.statement: Ending Red Cloud's War, the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty (dated 29 April 1868; bands signed through the year) created the Great Sioux Reservation including the Black Hills, closed the Bozeman Trail forts, and reserved unceded hunting territory to the west.

citations.title: Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) (National Archives Milestone Documents)
citations.quote: signed on April 29, 1868, between the U.S. Government and the Sioux Nation, the United States recognized the Black Hills

citations.title: The Treaties of Fort Laramie, 1851 & 1868 (North Dakota Studies, State Historical Society of North Dakota)
citations.quote: The treaty created the Great Sioux Reservation (in gray).

events.notes: The treaty required signatures of three-fourths of adult males for cession; the Crow made a separate treaty at Fort Laramie on 7 May 1868.

events.title: Battle of the Washita River (Washita massacre)
events.statement: On 27 November 1868 Lt. Col. George Custer's 7th Cavalry attacked Black Kettle's Southern Cheyenne camp on the Washita River in Indian Territory; Black Kettle, a peace chief who had survived Sand Creek, was killed.

citations.title: Battle of Washita River (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: occurred on November 27, 1868, when Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer's 7th U.S. Cavalry attacked Black Kettle's Southern Cheyenne camp on the Washita River

citations.title: History & Culture (Washita Battlefield National Historic Site, National Park Service)
citations.quote: the attack by Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer and his 7th US Cavalry on the Cheyenne encampment of Peace Chief Black Kettle

events.title: Red River War begins: Second Battle of Adobe Walls
events.statement: On 27 June 1874 about 700 Comanche, Kiowa, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors, led by Quanah Parker and the medicine man Isa-tai, attacked buffalo hunters at Adobe Walls in the Texas Panhandle, opening the Red River War that ended with Quanah Parker's band coming into Fort Sill on 2 June 1875.

citations.title: Red River War (1874-1875) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The Indians' attack at Adobe Walls may be considered the official beginning of the Red River War.

citations.title: Parker, Quanah (Handbook of Texas)
citations.quote: this alliance of some 700 warriors

citations.title: Second Battle of Adobe Walls (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was fought on June 27, 1874

events.notes: Hunters were killing the southern bison herds that the nations depended on. The war's decisive engagement was at Palo Duro Canyon (Sept 1874).

events.title: Battle of the Little Bighorn (Greasy Grass)
events.statement: On 25-26 June 1876 Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors defeated the US 7th Cavalry under Lt. Col. Custer along the Little Bighorn River in Montana; the army was accompanied by Crow and Arikara scouts.

citations.title: Story of the Battle (Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: fought along the ridges, steep bluffs, and ravines of the Little Bighorn River, in south-central Montana on June 25-26, 1876

citations.title: Battle of the Little Bighorn (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It took place on June 25-26, 1876

events.notes: Battle spanned two days (25-26 June); dated to day 25.

events.title: Black Hills taken by the Act of 28 February 1877
