events.statement: Congress cut off Sioux rations until they ceded the Black Hills, then on 28 February 1877 enacted an 'agreement' signed by only a small share of adult Lakota men, removing the Black Hills from the Great Sioux Reservation; the Supreme Court held in 1980 that this was a taking requiring just compensation.

citations.title: Black Hills land claim (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: officially removed the Black Hills from the Sioux Reservation by passing the Congressional Act of February 28, 1877

citations.title: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980) (Legal Information Institute)
citations.quote: In 1877, Congress passed an Act (1877 Act) implementing this

events.notes: The 1868 treaty required three-fourths of adult male signatures for cessions; the 1876 agreement was signed by only about 10% (Supreme Court summary). The Sioux Nation has refused the monetary award.

events.title: Wounded Knee massacre
events.statement: On 29 December 1890 the US 7th Cavalry killed at least 146, and by most later estimates 250 to 300, Lakota men, women and children at Wounded Knee Creek on Pine Ridge Reservation, during the disarming of Spotted Elk's (Big Foot's) Miniconjou band.

citations.title: Wounded Knee Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The event occurred on December 29, 1890, near Wounded Knee Creek

citations.title: U.S. Army massacres Lakota Indians at Wounded Knee (HISTORY)
citations.quote: the U.S. Cavalry kills 146 Lakota Indians at Wounded Knee on the Pine Ridge reservation in South Dakota

events.notes: Casualty figures differ: 146 (HISTORY.com) vs 250-300 (Wikipedia). Sitting Bull had been killed at Standing Rock on 15 December 1890.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic of 1837 on the Upper Missouri
events.statement: Smallpox carried up the Missouri River on an American Fur Company steamboat in 1837 devastated the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara, reducing the Mandan to as few as 125 survivors.

citations.title: Mandan (Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site, National Park Service)
citations.quote: an 1837 smallpox epidemic reduced the Mandan to as few as 125 individuals

citations.title: 1837 Great Plains smallpox epidemic (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: carried infected people and supplies up the Missouri River

events.notes: MHA Nation history says survivors numbered 125; the epidemic affected many other nations on the Upper Missouri.

events.title: Spanish-Comanche peace treaty (Anza)
events.statement: After Governor Juan Bautista de Anza's 1783 campaign and 1784 peace overtures, a formal peace was concluded at Pecos Pueblo on 28 February 1786, opening the Comanchero trade; Texas had a separate Spanish-Comanche treaty in 1785.

citations.title: Juan Bautista de Anza (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: a formal treaty was concluded on 28 February 1786 at Pecos Pueblo

citations.title: Comanche Indians (Handbook of Texas)
citations.quote: The result was the Spanish-Comanche Treaty of 1785

events.notes: Conflict: Handbook of Texas dates the Spanish-Comanche peace in Texas to 1785; Anza's New Mexico treaty is dated 1786.

events.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Dull Knife and Little Wolf)
events.statement: On 9-10 September 1878 about 350 Northern Cheyenne led by Little Wolf and Dull Knife left the Darlington reservation in Indian Territory to return north; the group that surrendered at Fort Robinson, Nebraska, was confined and in January 1879 broke out and was largely killed or recaptured.

citations.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In the early morning of September 10 the band fled up the North Canadian River.

citations.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In January 1879 they escaped from their confinement and fled north.

events.notes: Wikipedia only. Group totals: 353 left; some reached Montana, where the Northern Cheyenne Reservation was set aside in 1884.

events.title: Ponca removal to Indian Territory
events.statement: In 1877 the United States forcibly removed the Ponca from their reservation at the Niobrara to Indian Territory, without the consent of the Ponca chiefs and without adequate facilities; Standing Bear's return north led to Standing Bear v. Crook (1879).

citations.title: Ponca (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: the federal government removed the Ponca to Indian Territory in 1877

citations.title: Ponca (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the United States forcibly removed the Ponca people from the Ponca Reservation in the Dakota Territory to the Indian Territory

events.notes: Months of the removal vary by source and are omitted.

events.title: Battle of Seven Oaks (Victory of the Frog Plain)
events.statement: Métis and First Nations men led by Cuthbert Grant, carrying pemmican to North West Company canoe brigades, were confronted at Seven Oaks by HBC governor Robert Semple and 28 men; Semple and 20 of his party were killed along with one Métis.

citations.title: Battle of Seven Oaks (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The Battle of Seven Oaks, or the Victory of the Frog Plain (la Victoire de la Grenouillère), took place 19 June 1816.

citations.title: Battle of Seven Oaks (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The gunfire and hand-to-hand combat that resulted left Semple and 20 of the HBC party dead.

events.notes: Climax of the Pemmican Wars; the Métis call it the Victory of the Frog Plain.

events.title: Selkirk Treaty (Peguis and Lord Selkirk)

place.name: Fort Garry (The Forks, Red River Settlement)

events.statement: Peguis and four other Saulteaux and Cree chiefs signed a treaty with Lord Selkirk granting a strip of land two miles wide on each side of the Red and Assiniboine rivers for the Red River settlement, for an annual payment of tobacco.

citations.title: Peguis - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: On 18 July 1817 Peguis was one of five Saulteaux and Cree chiefs who signed a treaty with Lord Selkirk

citations.title: Peguis First Nation (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty allocated land along the Red and Assiniboine Rivers to Lord Selkirk and his settlers for an annual rent of tobacco.

events.notes: Other sources (Manitoba Historical Society) give 20 July 1817; the Dictionary of Canadian Biography's 18 July used. The signing place is not given; the point marks the confluence at which the ceded strip began.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic of 1781-82 on the Hudson Bay and western plains
events.statement: A smallpox epidemic spread through fur trade posts and Indigenous camps in the winter of 1781-82; the Denesuline, who traded at Hudson's Bay Company posts, were among the hardest hit.

citations.title: Denesuline (Chipewyan) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Epidemics of European diseases decimated the population, with the first great smallpox epidemic occurring in 1781-82

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Three (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)
citations.quote: The winter of 1781-82 proved horribly devastating to the Aboriginal people of western Canada.

events.notes: Samuel Hearne guessed that as many as 9 in 10 of the Chipewyan trading at the Hudson's Bay posts died (as quoted by historian Michael Payne in the Alberta Online Encyclopedia); this is an eyewitness estimate. Event year is 1781 (the winter began in 1781).

events.title: Smallpox epidemic of 1837-38 on the northern plains
events.statement: Smallpox carried up the Missouri River on the American Fur Company steamboat St. Peter's spread to the Niitsitapi (Blackfoot Confederacy), of whom about 6,000 are said to have died; the outbreak also spread north into Canada.

citations.title: Blackfoot Confederacy (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Niitsitapi contracted the disease and eventually 6,000 died, marking an end to their dominance among tribes over the Plains.

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Five (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)
citations.quote: There was a pretty significant outbreak in 1837-38, when smallpox was transmitted along the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers into the West

events.notes: The 6,000 figure rests on Wikipedia only. Place is Fort Union, the steamboat's destination (Wikipedia).

events.title: Marias Massacre (Baker Massacre)
events.statement: US Army troops under Major Eugene Baker attacked a camp of Piikani (Piegan) Blackfeet led by Heavy Runner on the Marias River; about 200 or more people, mostly women, children and elders, were killed, and many in the camp were sick with smallpox.

citations.title: Marias Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The massacre occurred on January 23, 1870, in Montana Territory.

citations.title: Marias Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Approximately 200 Native people were killed, most of whom were women, children, and older men.

citations.title: Who are the Piikani? (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: About 220 Piegans died in 1870 as a result of the conflict.

events.notes: Death toll varies by source (Army report lower; The Canadian Encyclopedia says about 220 Piegans died). Some Piikani moved to Canada afterwards and signed Treaty 7.

events.title: Treaty 1 (Stone Fort Treaty) signed at Lower Fort Garry
events.statement: Treaty 1, the first Numbered Treaty, was concluded on 3 August 1871 at Lower Fort Garry between the Crown and Anishinaabe (Saulteaux) and Swampy Cree chiefs, after eight days of negotiation.

citations.title: Treaty 1 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: is an agreement established on August 3, 1871, between the Crown and the Anishinaabe and Swampy Cree

citations.title: Events in Manitoba History: Treaty 1 (August 1871) (Manitoba Historical Society)
citations.quote: Events in Manitoba History: Treaty 1 (August 1871)

events.notes: The Manitoba Historical Society lists the signatory First Nations as Brokenhead, Long Plain, Peguis, Roseau River, Sagkeeng, Sandy Bay and Swan Lake.

events.title: Cypress Hills Massacre
events.statement: American wolf hunters and whisky traders attacked an Assiniboine (Nakoda) camp near Battle Creek in the Cypress Hills; the killing prompted the rapid creation of the North-West Mounted Police.

citations.title: Cypress Hills massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Cypress Hills Massacre occurred on June 1, 1873, near Battle Creek in the Cypress Hills region

citations.title: North-West Mounted Police (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: In June 1873, more than 30 Assiniboine were killed near a whiskey post in an incident known as the Cypress Hills Massacre.

citations.title: Cypress Hills (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: in 1873 a gang of American wolf hunters massacred some Assiniboine there

events.notes: Death tolls differ: Wikipedia says thirteen or more Assiniboine warriors died; the Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation article says 20; The Canadian Encyclopedia says more than 30. Sources in the catalogue are not unanimous; no figure is asserted.

events.title: Treaty 4 (Qu'Appelle Treaty)
events.statement: Treaty 4 was signed at Fort Qu'Appelle on 15 September 1874 by Cree, Saulteaux and Assiniboine bands; Canada treats it as a cession of most of southern Saskatchewan along with portions of western Manitoba and southern Alberta.

citations.title: Treaty 4 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Treaty 4 - also known as the Qu'Appelle Treaty - was signed on 15 September 1874 at Fort Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan.

citations.title: Treaty 4 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The majority of Treaty 4 lands are in present-day southern Saskatchewan.

events.notes: Assiniboine bands from the Cypress Hills adhered later, at Fort Walsh on 25 September 1877.

events.title: Treaty 6 signed at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt
events.statement: Treaty 6 was signed by Cree, Assiniboine and Ojibwe leaders on 23 August 1876 at Fort Carlton and on 9 September at Fort Pitt; Pitikwahanapiwiyin (Poundmaker) objected, and Mistahimaskwa (Big Bear) was absent.

citations.title: Treaty 6 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Treaty 6 was signed by Crown representatives and Cree, Assiniboine and Ojibwe leaders on 23 August 1876 at Fort Carlton

citations.title: Treaty 6 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: This is our land, it isn't a piece of pemmican to be cut off and given in little pieces back to us.

events.notes: Treaty 6 added a medicine chest, more agricultural implements and a 'famine and pestilence' clause. Big Bear adhered in 1882 (Wikipedia).

events.title: Treaty 7 signed at Blackfoot Crossing
events.statement: Treaty 7 was signed by the Siksika, Kainai, Piikani, Stoney-Nakoda and Tsuut'ina at Blackfoot Crossing on 22 September 1877; the nations understood it as a peace treaty and not a land surrender.

citations.title: Treaty 7 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: It was signed on 22 September 1877 by five First Nations: the Siksika (Blackfoot), Kainai (Blood), Piikani (Peigan), Stoney-Nakoda, and Tsuut'ina (Sarcee).

citations.title: About - Siksika Nation (official site)
citations.quote: Treaty Number 7 was signed at Blackfoot Crossing in Siksika.

events.notes: The Tsuut'ina (Sarcee), who became allied with the Confederacy later and speak an unrelated language (Wikipedia, Piikani Nation), are not catalogued separately here.

events.title: Frog Lake Massacre
events.statement: Cree men of Mistahimaskwa's (Big Bear's) band, led by war chief Wandering Spirit, killed nine officials, clergy and settlers at Frog Lake, in the first days of the North-West Resistance; Big Bear tried to stop the violence.

citations.title: Frog Lake massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Led by Wandering Spirit, Cree men attacked and killed nine officials, clergy and settlers in the small settlement of Frog Lake

citations.title: North-West Resistance (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: On Thursday 2 April, war chief Wandering Spirit shot and killed federal Indian agent Thomas Quinn.

events.notes: The warrior society acted against Big Bear's wishes according to The Canadian Encyclopedia; the band had been pressed by the cutting off of rations.

events.title: Battle of Cut Knife
events.statement: Cree and Assiniboine resistors defeated 300 soldiers under Lieutenant-Colonel William Otter at Cut Knife Hill, on Pitikwahanapiwiyin's (Poundmaker's) reserve; Poundmaker later surrendered and was convicted of treason.

citations.title: North-West Resistance (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: On 1 May, Colonel Otter moved west from Battleford with 300 men and early the next day confronted the Cree and Assiniboine force

citations.title: Battle of Cut Knife (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: On 2 May 1885, during the North-West Resistance, Cree and Assiniboine resistors defeated 300 soldiers commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel William Otter

events.notes: Poundmaker surrendered on 26 May 1885 (Wikipedia, Battle of Batoche article).

events.title: Battle of Batoche
events.statement: Canadian militia under General Frederick Middleton attacked the Métis capital of Batoche from 9 to 12 May 1885 and overcame the defenders led by Gabriel Dumont and Louis Riel, ending the North-West Resistance.

citations.title: Battle of Batoche (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Fought from May 9 to 12, 1885

citations.title: Batoche (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The village of Batoche was captured by the federal forces, and the spirit of the resistance broken.

events.notes: The battle ended on 12 May 1885; Riel surrendered on 15 May.

events.title: Louis Riel hanged at Regina
events.statement: Louis Riel, leader of the Red River Resistance and the 1885 North-West Resistance, was executed for high treason at Regina on 16 November 1885.

citations.title: Louis Riel (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: died 16 November 1885 in Regina, SK

citations.title: Louis Riel (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: was executed for high treason for his role in the 1885 resistance to Canadian encroachment on Métis lands

events.title: Manitoba Act passed; Manitoba admitted to Confederation

place.name: Fort Garry (The Forks, Red River Settlement)

events.statement: The Manitoba Act, born of the Red River Resistance and the Métis provisional government's negotiations, became law on 12 May 1870 and created the province of Manitoba with commitments including a 1.4 million acre land reserve for Métis families.

citations.title: Manitoba Act (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: It received royal assent and became law on 12 May 1870.

citations.title: Métis (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: including a 1.4 million acre land reserve

events.notes: The Act was passed in Ottawa; the place point marks the Red River Settlement it concerned. Métis leaders argue the original negotiated agreement was never properly implemented (The Canadian Encyclopedia).

events.title: Treaty 8: first signing at Lesser Slave Lake
events.statement: Treaty 8 was first signed on 21 June 1899 at Lesser Slave Lake with Cree representatives, and was then taken to Denesuline, Dane-zaa and other peoples across northern Alberta, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia.

citations.title: Treaty 8 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Treaty 8 was signed on 21 June 1899 by the Crown and First Nations of the Lesser Slave Lake area.

citations.title: Treaty 8 (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The first signing of Treaty 8 occurred at Lesser Slave Lake on 21 June 1899

events.notes: Further adhesions: Fort Chipewyan 13 July 1899; Fort Resolution 25 July 1900 (Wikipedia).

events.title: Champlain-Innu alliance at Tadoussac
events.statement: Samuel de Champlain formed an alliance with an Innu group in 1603, laying a foundation for French-Indigenous relations in the St. Lawrence valley.

citations.title: Innu (Montagnais-Naskapi) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Champlain formed an alliance with an Innu group in 1603, laying a foundation for French-Indigenous relations to come.

events.notes: The Canadian Encyclopedia ties the alliance to the Tadoussac region; the exact meeting place is not stated in the quoted passage.

events.title: Founding of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy (Great Law of Peace)
events.statement: The Peacemaker and Hiawatha (Aionwatha) united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca under the Great Law of Peace, with the council fire kept at Onondaga; the date is contested.

citations.title: History - Onondaga Nation
citations.quote: Over a thousand years ago on the shores of Onondaga Lake, in present day central New York, democracy was born.

citations.title: Who We Are - Haudenosaunee Confederacy
citations.quote: The exact date of the joining of the nations is unknown and said to be time immemorial

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Estimates vary widely as to the founding date of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, with many claiming a date in the mid-16th century.

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: in 1997, researchers Barbara A. Mann and Jerry L. Fields proposed a founding date of 31 August 1142.

citations.title: Who We Are - Haudenosaunee Confederacy
citations.quote: The confederacy was founded by the prophet known as the Peacemaker with the help of Aionwatha, more commonly known as Hiawatha.

events.notes: DATE CONTESTED: Haudenosaunee Confederacy - unknown/'time immemorial'; Onondaga Nation - 'over a thousand years ago'; The Canadian Encyclopedia - many claim mid-16th century, Mann and Fields propose 31 Aug 1142; Wikipedia's Great Law of Peace article states both c.1102 CE and c.1190 in its first paragraphs. 1142 (circa) is used only as the most specific scholarly proposal in the cited sources.

events.title: Tuscarora join the Confederacy; the Five Nations become the Six Nations

place.name: Onondaga Nation territory (council fire of the Confederacy)

events.statement: Pushed from their Carolina homelands by British colonial expansion, the Tuscarora sought refuge with the Haudenosaunee in 1722 and were accepted as the sixth nation of the Confederacy.

citations.title: Six Nations of the Grand River - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The Tuscarora sought refuge with the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in 1722, as a result of British colonial expansion into their homelands in the Carolinas.

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The linguistically related Tuscarora moved north from North Carolina and Virginia to join the confederacy in 1722.

citations.title: Six Nations of the Grand River - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Later that year, they were accepted as the Confederacy's sixth nation.

events.notes: The Tuscarora (a Southeast-region nation) present their issues to the Confederacy through the Cayuga.

events.title: Beaver Wars (Iroquois Wars; French and Iroquois Wars)
events.statement: A series of intermittent conflicts over the fur trade in the Great Lakes and St Lawrence regions in which the Haudenosaunee, supported by the Dutch and later the English, fought Wendat and other French-allied nations; the Wendat were dispersed after 1649 and the wars ended with the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701.

citations.title: Beaver Wars
citations.quote: a series of intermittent conflicts fought in the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River regions of North America from 1609 to 1701.

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The French-allied Huron-Wendat were dispersed from their homeland after several villages were destroyed in 1649 and multiple individuals were adopted into the Haudenosaunee.

citations.title: Beaver Wars
citations.quote: The wars pitted the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), supported by the Dutch and later the English

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: With the coming of the fur trade in the 16th century, the Haudenosaunee embarked on successful campaigns to subjugate or disperse neighbouring groups.

events.notes: Start date varies: Wikipedia dates the wars 1609-1701; many accounts date the intense phase to the 1640s onward (Wendat villages destroyed 1649). Place is a representative anchor (Montreal) for a war spanning the Great Lakes and St Lawrence.

events.title: Great Peace of Montreal
events.statement: On 4 August 1701 the governor of New France and representatives of 39 Indigenous nations, including the Haudenosaunee, signed a peace ending the Beaver Wars.

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal
citations.quote: It was signed on August 4, 1701, by Louis-Hector de Callière, governor of New France, and 1300 representatives of 39 Indigenous nations.

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Later the same year in Montréal, Haudenosaunee signed a treaty with the French, ensuring peace among Indigenous nations and further protection.

events.notes: Participant list is indicative; the treaty involved about 39 nations. The Haudenosaunee also concluded a separate treaty at Albany with the British in 1701.

events.title: Albany Congress
events.statement: From 19 June to 11 July 1754 delegates from seven British colonies met at Albany with Native leaders, including the Haudenosaunee, to discuss relations with Native nations and defence against the French; the Haudenosaunee also agreed to sell a large Pennsylvania tract (the Albany Purchase).

citations.title: Albany Congress
citations.quote: The Albany Congress (June 19 - July 11, 1754), also known as the Albany Convention of 1754

citations.title: Treaty of Easton
citations.quote: In 1754, at the Albany Congress, the Haudenosaunee agreed to sell to Pennsylvania a huge tract of land west of the Susquehanna River.

events.notes: The Albany Purchase was later disputed and Pennsylvania returned the land west of the Alleghenies in 1758 (Treaty of Easton).

events.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1768)
events.statement: On 5 November 1768 the Haudenosaunee and Britain signed a treaty at Fort Stanwix that set a Line of Property down the Ohio River, ceding lands claimed by the Shawnee, Lenape and others who were not signatories.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix
citations.quote: The final treaty was signed on November 5 with one signatory for each of the Six Nations

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix
citations.quote: The treaty established a Line of Property following the Ohio River that ceded the Kentucky portion of the Virginia Colony to the British Crown

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix
citations.quote: primarily the Shawnee and Lenape, were present at the negotiations in 1768, they were not signatories.

events.notes: Quotes are from the Wikipedia article. The Shawnee and Lenape were present but not signatories and disputed the cession.

events.title: Sullivan Expedition (Sullivan-Clinton Campaign)
events.statement: In summer 1779 Continental Army brigades under General John Sullivan razed about 40 Haudenosaunee villages and their crops in central New York; over 5,000 Haudenosaunee fled to Fort Niagara.

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition
citations.quote: The expedition was largely successful, with 40 Haudenosaunee villages razed and their crops and food stores destroyed.

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition
citations.quote: beginning on June 18 when the army marched from Easton, Pennsylvania

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: many Seneca, Onondaga and Cayuga towns were burned in 1779

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition
citations.quote: The campaign drove just over 5,000 Haudenosaunee to Fort Niagara seeking British protection, and depopulated the area for post-war settlement.

events.notes: Place is the expedition's one major battlefield (Newtown, 29 Aug 1779) as an anchor for a campaign across Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga country. Some scholars call the campaign genocide; the term is disputed.

events.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784)
events.statement: On 22 October 1784 delegates of the Six Nations and the United States signed a treaty at Fort Stanwix by which the Confederacy gave up claims to the Ohio country and lands along the Niagara River; the Six Nations council at Buffalo Creek refused to ratify it.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784)
citations.quote: The Treaty of Fort Stanwix was a treaty finalized on October 22, 1784

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784)
citations.quote: the Haudenosaunee Confederacy ceded all claims to the Ohio territory, a strip of land along the Niagara river

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784)
citations.quote: The Six Nations council at Buffalo Creek refused to ratify the treaty

events.notes: Joseph Brant and other Confederacy leaders did not accept that the delegates had authority to cede land.

events.title: Haldimand Proclamation (Grand River grant)

place.name: Six Nations of the Grand River (Haldimand Tract)

events.statement: On 25 October 1784 Governor Frederick Haldimand granted the Mohawk and other Five Nations allies of the Crown land six miles deep on each side of the Grand River, now Six Nations of the Grand River.

citations.title: Haldimand Proclamation
citations.quote: The decree was issued by the Governor of the Province of Quebec, Frederick Haldimand, on October 25, 1784

citations.title: Six Nations of the Grand River - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea) was able to secure a tract of land for the Haudenosaunee Confederacy from Sir Frederick Haldimand

events.title: Treaty of Canandaigua (Pickering Treaty)
events.statement: On 11 November 1794 about fifty Haudenosaunee chiefs and war chiefs and US agent Timothy Pickering signed the Treaty of Canandaigua, establishing perpetual peace and friendship and confirming Haudenosaunee lands in New York.

citations.title: Treaty of Canandaigua
citations.quote: It was signed at Canandaigua, New York, on November 11, 1794, by fifty royaner (hoya:ne:h) and war chiefs

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition
citations.quote: The November 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua established perpetual "peace and friendship" between the Haudenosaunee and the United States

events.notes: The Treaty is still honoured by the Haudenosaunee and the United States each year.

events.title: Treaty of Big Tree (Seneca land sale)
events.statement: At Big Tree (Geneseo) in August-September 1797 the Seneca Nation sold nearly all their homeland west of the Genesee River, about 3.5 million acres, reserving twelve small tracts.

citations.title: Treaty of Big Tree
citations.quote: in which the Seneca relinquished their rights to nearly all of their traditional homeland in New York State-nearly 3.5 million acres

citations.title: Treaty of Big Tree
citations.quote: The delegates for both parties met from August 20, 1797, until September 16, 1797

events.title: Treaties of Buffalo Creek (1838, 1842): Seneca removal treaties
events.statement: The 1838 Treaty of Buffalo Creek, obtained from 43 of more than 80 Seneca chiefs, required the Seneca to give up their New York reservations and move west; after protest a new treaty ratified in 1842 let them keep Cattaraugus and Allegany but dissolved the Buffalo Creek Reservation.

citations.title: Treaty of Buffalo Creek
citations.quote: Second Treaty of Buffalo Creek (1838)

citations.title: Buffalo Creek Reservation
citations.quote: bribed, intimidated and deceived 43 of the more than 80 Seneca chiefs to agree to the Treaty of Buffalo Creek

citations.title: Buffalo Creek Reservation
citations.quote: the US negotiated a new treaty, which the Senate ratified in 1842.

citations.title: Buffalo Creek Reservation
citations.quote: the Seneca were allowed to keep their Cattaraugus, Oil Springs, Allegany and Tonawanda reservations after legal battles in the 1850s

events.notes: Wikipedia describes the 1838 treaty as part of the Jacksonian Indian Removal policy. Only the year of the 1838 treaty is given in the cited text.

events.title: French expedition destroys Seneca towns (Denonville, 1687)
events.statement: In summer 1687 the Marquis de Denonville led French regulars, Canadian militia and Native allies against the Seneca; the Seneca fired Ganondagan and fled as the army arrived.

citations.title: Ganondagan
citations.quote: On June 13, 1687, the Marquis de Denonville led an army from Canada

citations.title: Ganondagan
citations.quote: the Seneca "came to reconnoiter us and then went to burn their village and take to flight."

citations.title: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: France attacked Haudenosaunee towns in 1666, 1687, 1693 and 1696.

citations.title: Ganondagan
citations.quote: which consisted of 832 colonial regulars, more than 900 Canadian militia, and some 400 Indian allies

events.notes: The army set out on 13 June 1687; Ganondagan was found burned on 14 July (per Denonville).

events.title: Treaty of Shackamaxon (Penn's Treaty)
events.statement: William Penn and the Lenape leader Tamanend are said to have made a treaty of peace and friendship at Shackamaxon in 1682; no paper record survives.

citations.title: Treaty of Shackamaxon
citations.quote: was a treaty between William Penn and Tamanend of the Lenape signed in 1682.

citations.title: History - Delaware Nation
citations.quote: But there are no surviving paper documents from this agreement.

events.notes: The Delaware Nation notes Penn 'allegedly' made the treaty and that his intention was still to acquire Lenape land; the wampum belt tradition is later. Wikipedia gives 1682 but Penn arrived in late October 1682, and some accounts place it in 1683.

events.title: Peach War: Munsee Lenape occupy New Amsterdam
events.statement: On 15 September 1655 several hundred Munsee Lenape landed at New Amsterdam in a one-day occupation, followed by raids on Staten Island and Pavonia (Jersey City).

citations.title: Peach War
citations.quote: The Peach War, sometimes called the Peach Tree War, was a one-day occupation of New Amsterdam on September 15, 1655, by several hundred Munsee

events.notes: Some writers speculate that the Peach War was orchestrated by the Susquehannock in response to the Dutch conquest of New Sweden.

events.title: First Esopus War
events.statement: The Esopus, a Munsee Lenape people of the Kingston area, fought Dutch settlers from 20 September 1659 to 15 July 1660, the first of the two Esopus Wars.

citations.title: Esopus Wars
citations.quote: The First Esopus War was a short-lived conflict between Dutch settlers and the Esopus Natives from September 20, 1659 and July 15, 1660.

events.notes: Wikipedia; the second war was fought 1663-1664.

events.title: Walking Purchase
events.statement: On 19 September 1737 Pennsylvania's walkers covered a day-and-a-half 'walk' that the Penn family used to claim about 1.2 million acres of Lenape land in the Lehigh Valley and upper Delaware.

citations.title: Walking Purchase
citations.quote: The walk occurred on September 19, 1737

citations.title: History - Delaware Nation
citations.quote: In 1737 Penn's sons met with the Lenape and presented an illegitimate treaty supposedly signed with William Penn decades earlier

events.notes: The Delaware Nation, which calls the purchase fraudulent, says the Lenape were forced into Ohio as a result.

events.title: Treaty of Easton (1758)
events.statement: At Easton, Pennsylvania, in October 1758, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, the Haudenosaunee and the Lenape met; Pennsylvania returned the land west of the Alleghenies bought at Albany in 1754, removing a cause of Lenape raiding in the French and Indian War.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton
citations.quote: The Treaty of Easton was a series of meetings held at Easton, Pennsylvania, from 7 to 26 October 1758

citations.title: Treaty of Easton
citations.quote: Pennsylvania agreed to return all of the land west of the Allegheny Mountains that it had acquired in the 1754 Albany Purchase

citations.title: Treaty of Easton
citations.quote: thus eliminating a major reason for Lenape raids during the French and Indian War.

events.notes: Meetings ran 7-26 October 1758; month precision used. Teedyuscung and the Pennsylvania governor had also formalized peace with the eastern Lenape by an earlier exchange of wampum belts.

events.title: Treaty of Fort Pitt (1778)
events.statement: On 17 September 1778 Lenape leaders White Eyes, Captain John Killbuck Jr. and Captain Pipe signed the first treaty between the United States and a Native nation; the promises of land and a state were not kept.

citations.title: History - Delaware Nation
citations.quote: White Eyes was instrumental in establishing the Fort Pitt Treaty, which he signed on September 17th, 1778

citations.title: History - Delaware Nation
citations.quote: the 1778 Fort Pitt Treaty was both the first U.S treaty signed with and broken with a Native Nation

events.title: Gnadenhutten massacre
events.statement: On 8 March 1782 Pennsylvania militiamen under David Williamson killed 96 pacifist Moravian Christian Indians, primarily Lenape and Mohican, at Gnadenhutten, Ohio.

citations.title: Gnadenhutten massacre
citations.quote: the killing of 96 pacifist Moravian Christian Indians (primarily Lenape and Mohican) by U.S. militiamen from Pennsylvania

citations.title: History - Delaware Nation
citations.quote: On March 8th 1782, American militiamen slaughtered 96 Lenape elders, men, women, children, and infants at Gnadenhutten, Ohio

events.title: Delaware Tribe of Indians relocate to the Cherokee Nation (1867)
events.statement: Under an 1867 agreement the ancestors of the Delaware Tribe of Indians relocated to the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory.

citations.title: Delaware Tribe of Indians
citations.quote: the ancestors of the Delaware Tribe of Indians agreed in 1867 to relocate to the Cherokee Nation in what was then Indian Territory.

citations.title: Delaware Tribe of Indians
citations.quote: the Lenape were forced to cede their Eastern lands and moved first to Ohio and later to Indiana (Plainfield), Missouri, Kansas, and Indian Territory

events.notes: Place is the Tribe's present seat at Bartlesville; Wikipedia says the Tribe agreed to relocate in 1867.

events.title: Jamestown founded within Powhatan territory
events.statement: In May 1607 English colonists founded Jamestown inside the territory of the Powhatan Confederacy, led by Wahunsenacawh (Chief Powhatan).

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: The settlement at Jamestown, Virginia, was established in May 1607 within the territory of the Powhatan

events.title: First Anglo-Powhatan War
events.statement: The first of three wars between the Powhatan Confederacy and the Virginia Company colonists began in 1609 and ended with a peace in 1614; Governor De La Warr's men burned Paspahegh town on 9 August 1610.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: The first war started in 1609 and ended in a peace settlement in 1614.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: De La Warr sent George Percy and James Davis with 70 men to attack the Paspahegh town on August 9, 1610

events.notes: Start date: Wikipedia's lede says 1609; many accounts date the war 1610-1614. Ended with the 'Peace of Pocahontas' in 1614.

events.title: Powhatan attack of 22 March 1622 (Second Anglo-Powhatan War begins)
events.statement: On 22 March 1622 Opechancanough's warriors struck the English settlements without warning, killing hundreds of colonists and opening the second war (1622-1632).

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: his warriors struck without warning on March 22, 1622, from where they had been planted among the settlements, and killed hundreds

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: The second war lasted from 1622 to 1632.

events.title: Third Anglo-Powhatan War
events.statement: On 18 April 1644 Opechancanough and the remnants of the Powhatan Confederacy tried once more to drive out the settlers; he was captured in 1646 and killed in captivity.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: another Anglo-Powhatan War began on April 18, 1644, as the remnants of the Powhatan Confederacy under Opechancanough

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: The third war lasted from 1644 until 1646 and ended when Opechancanough was captured and killed.

events.title: Treaty of 1646 (Necotowance and Virginia)
events.statement: In October 1646 Necotowance, successor to Opechancanough, signed a peace with Virginia that ended the Third Anglo-Powhatan War and forced the Powhatan out of the land between the York and James rivers.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: In October 1646 the General Assembly of Virginia signed a peace treaty with Necotowance which brought the Third Anglo-Powhatan War to an end.

citations.title: Pamunkey Reservation on the Middle Peninsula - Virginia Places
citations.quote: Necotowance agreed to vacate the Peninsula between the James and York rivers.

events.title: Treaty of Middle Plantation (1677)
events.statement: Cockacoeske, Queen of the Pamunkey, and leaders of other Virginia Native nations signed the Treaty of 1677 with the English Crown after Bacon's Rebellion, which established Indian reservations.

citations.title: Treaty of Middle Plantation
citations.quote: was signed in Virginia on May 28, 1677, between the English Crown and representatives from Native American tribes in Virginia

citations.title: Treaty of Middle Plantation
citations.quote: Concluded the 29th day of May, 1677.

citations.title: Pamunkey Reservation on the Middle Peninsula - Virginia Places
citations.quote: The 1677 Treaty of Middle Plantation created an 6-mile wide, 18,000-acre exclusive Native American zone

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars
citations.quote: the Treaty of Middle Plantation which established Indian reservations following Bacon's Rebellion

citations.title: Treaty of Middle Plantation
citations.quote: The Queen of Pamunkey, known as Cockacoeske to the English

events.notes: DATE: the article's opening says signed 28 May 1677; the treaty text it reproduces says 'Concluded the 29th day of May, 1677'. 29 May is used.

events.title: Epidemic devastates the Wampanoag and the New England coast (1616-1619)
events.statement: From about 1615 to 1619 epidemic disease, carried on European ships, dramatically reduced the Wampanoag and neighbouring peoples; the Patuxet were wiped out and the Narragansett largely escaped.

citations.title: Wampanoag
citations.quote: From 1615 to 1619, a leptospirosis epidemic carried by rodents arriving in European ships dramatically reduced the population of the Wampanoag and neighboring tribes.

citations.title: Patuxet
citations.quote: The Patuxet were wiped out by a series of plagues that decimated the indigenous peoples of southeastern New England

citations.title: Narragansett - Encyclopedia.com
citations.quote: The Narragansett managed to escape the worst epidemics

events.notes: Sources give 1614-1620 (Patuxet), 1615-1619 (Wampanoag) and 1617 (Wabanaki Alliance, 'wiped out over 75 percent of the inhabitants along the New England coast'); the disease is attributed variously to leptospirosis, smallpox and other causes. The Massachusett people were also devastated (no separate polity entry in this catalogue).

events.title: Wampanoag treaty with Plymouth Colony (Massasoit)
events.statement: In spring 1621 the Massasoit and Plymouth Colony's governor John Carver agreed a treaty of peace and mutual aid, with Massasoit seeking an alliance against the Narragansett.

citations.title: Wampanoag treaty
citations.quote: The Wampanoag treaty was a treaty signed on April 1 [O.S. March 22], 1621 between the Wampanoag, led by Massasoit

citations.title: Massasoit
citations.quote: Outbreaks of an unidentified disease had devastated the Pokanokets, and Massasoit sought an alliance with the colonies of New England against the neighboring Narragansetts

citations.title: Wampanoag treaty
citations.quote: If any did unjustly war against him, we would aid him; if any did war against us, he should aid us.

events.notes: Date: April 1 (Gregorian) = March 22, 1621 (Old Style), as given in Wikipedia's lead. The peace lasted until King Philip's War.

events.title: King Philip's (Metacom's) War begins at Swansea
events.statement: King Philip's War began on 20 June 1675 with Pokanoket attacks on homesteads at Swansea, Plymouth Colony, and spread to the Nipmuc, Pocumtuc and Narragansett; on 28 June colonial troops destroyed the Wampanoag town at Mount Hope.

citations.title: King Philip's War
citations.quote: a band of Pokanokets attacked several isolated homesteads in the small Plymouth colony settlement of Swansea on June 20, 1675

citations.title: King Philip's War
citations.quote: a coalition of Algonquian tribes of the Northeastern Woodlands-the Wampanoags, the Pocomtucs, the Nipmucs, and the Narragansetts

citations.title: Roger Williams: King Philip's War - National Park Service
citations.quote: King Phillip sent the old men, women, and children of the tribe across Narragansett Bay to live safely with the Narragansett.

events.notes: The war is dated 1675-1676 (NPS, Encyclopedia.com) or 1675-1678 (Wikipedia, which includes the northern theatre). The first raid is dated 20 June (Wikipedia, citing Benjamin Church).

events.title: Metacom (King Philip) killed at Mount Hope
events.statement: On 12 August 1676 Metacom, Massasoit's son and chief sachem of the Wampanoag, was killed by colonial militia at Mount Hope.

citations.title: King Philip's War
citations.quote: On August 12, 1676, Metacom fled to Mount Hope where he was killed by the militia.

citations.title: King Philip's War
citations.quote: Hundreds of Wampanoags and their allies were publicly executed or enslaved, and the Wampanoags were left effectively landless.

citations.title: Massasoit
citations.quote: Massasoit's second son Metacom became sachem of the Pokanokets and chief sachem of the Greater Wampanoag Confederacy

events.title: Narragansett sachems grant land to Roger Williams (Providence)
events.statement: In 1636 the Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi gave land to Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts Bay, who founded Providence Plantations.

citations.title: Narragansett Indian Tribe
citations.quote: in 1636, Roger Williams acquired land from Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi and established Providence Plantations

citations.title: Narragansett - Encyclopedia.com
citations.quote: The Narragansett gave him land that became the city of Providence, Rhode Island.

events.title: Great Swamp Fight (Great Swamp Massacre)
events.statement: On 19 December 1675 colonial militia from Plymouth, Connecticut and Massachusetts Bay, including about 150 Pequots, attacked the Narragansett's principal winter settlement in the Great Swamp; hundreds of Narragansett men, women and children were killed.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight
citations.quote: Four days later, the Great Swamp Battle took place on the bitterly cold and stormy day of December 19, 1675.

citations.title: Roger Williams: King Philip's War - National Park Service
citations.quote: cost the lives of three hundred Native American men and almost four hundred women and children.

citations.title: Narragansett - Encyclopedia.com
citations.quote: On December 16, 1675, the colonial army laid siege to a Narragansett stronghold and destroyed it in what became known as the Great Swamp Fight.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight
citations.quote: The combined force of the New England militia included 150 Pequots

events.notes: Date: 19 Dec (Wikipedia) vs 16 Dec (Encyclopedia.com); the Narragansett had been pressed by the United Colonies for refusing to hand over Wampanoag refugees. NPS says the Narragansett refused with the words 'Not a Wampanoag nor the paring of a Wampanoag's nail.'

events.title: Pequot War begins

place.name: Mystic Fort (Pequot fort near the Mystic River)

events.statement: The Pequot War (1636-1638) began after the trader John Oldham was killed on a voyage to Block Island on 20 July 1636; English colonists of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Saybrook and their Narragansett and Mohegan allies fought the Pequot nation.

citations.title: Pequot War
citations.quote: the killing of a trader named John Oldham, who was attacked on a voyage to Block Island on July 20, 1636.

citations.title: Pequot War
citations.quote: The Pequot War was a conflict that took place in 1636 and ended in 1638 in New England

citations.title: Pequot War
citations.quote: a joint effort of the English colonists from the Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, and Saybrook colonies

events.notes: Wikipedia names the Oldham killing as a 'more proximate cause'; the war's roots lay in the fur trade and rivalry among the Pequot, Dutch, English, Narragansett and Mohegan. Place is the Pequot homeland at Mystic.

events.title: Mystic massacre (Battle of Mystic Fort)

place.name: Mystic Fort (Pequot fort near the Mystic River)

events.statement: On 26 May 1637 Connecticut forces under Captain John Mason and Narragansett and Mohegan allies set fire to the Pequot fort at Mystic, killing between 400 and 700 Pequots, most of them women, children and old people.

citations.title: Mystic massacre
citations.quote: took place on May 26, 1637 during the Pequot War

citations.title: Mystic massacre
citations.quote: There were between 400 and 700 Pequots killed during the attack

citations.title: Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation
citations.quote: Robin Cassasinnamon, the Pequots' first leader following the 1637 massacre at Mystick Fort.

citations.title: Pequot - Encyclopedia.com
citations.quote: Between three hundred and seven hundred Pequot, mostly women, children, and the elderly, were trapped inside as the fort was set ablaze.

events.notes: Estimates of the dead vary; Encyclopedia.com gives 300-700.

events.title: Treaty of Hartford (1638)
events.statement: On 21 September 1638 Connecticut, the Mohegan and the Narragansett concluded a treaty ending the Pequot War which divided the Pequot survivors, outlawed the Pequot name and gave Pequot land to the Connecticut River towns.

citations.title: Treaty of Hartford (1638)
citations.quote: concluded between English colonists in Connecticut, the Mohegan nation and the Narragansett nation on September 21, 1638

citations.title: Treaty of Hartford (1638)
citations.quote: The other major feature of this treaty was to outlaw the Pequot name.

citations.title: Treaty of Hartford (1638)
citations.quote: Surviving Pequot prisoners were divided between the tribes

events.notes: Massachusetts Bay was not a party and disputed Connecticut's claim to Pequot land. In 2025 a Connecticut state senator proposed a resolution condemning the treaty.

events.title: Narragansett siege of Fort Shantok
events.statement: In 1645 Uncas and the Mohegans were besieged by the Narragansett at Fort Shantok and were saved when the English brought supplies.

citations.title: Uncas
citations.quote: In 1645, Uncas and the Mohegans were under siege in Fort Shantok at Shattuck's Point

citations.title: Mohegan - Encyclopedia.com
citations.quote: The Narragansetts retaliated, attempting to starve the Mohegans out of their fortified village of Shantok until provisions were secretly brought in by the English.

events.notes: The Narragansett-Mohegan rivalry followed the Pequot War and the 1643 execution of the Narragansett sachem Miantonomi.

events.title: Wabanaki Confederacy formed at the Caughnawaga Council
events.statement: At a Caughnawaga Council in Mohawk territory in the 1680s, Eastern Algonquian peoples came together to form their own confederation, the Wabanaki Confederacy, according to Wikipedia and the Passamaquoddy wampum record.

citations.title: Wabanaki Confederacy
citations.quote: At one of these councils in the 1680s, the Eastern Algonquians came together to form their own confederation

events.notes: Single-source (Wikipedia); the Wabanaki Confederacy's own account may differ. The Caughnawaga Council met every three years in Mohawk territory; the place shown (Mohawk Valley) is approximate.

events.title: First Treaty of Casco (1678)
events.statement: On 12 April 1678 New York's government and Penobscot representatives under Chief Madockawando signed the first Treaty of Casco, ending the First Abenaki War; settlers were to pay corn rent and respect Penobscot land rights.

citations.title: Treaty of Casco (1678)
citations.quote: On 12 April 1678 the provincial government of New York, which controlled Maine between 1677 and 1686, signed the first Treaty of Casco

citations.title: Treaty of Casco (1678)
citations.quote: This land use tax symbolized continuing Abenaki sovereignty over Maine.

citations.title: Wabanaki Confederacy
citations.quote: The First Abenaki War ended with the Treaty of Casco

citations.title: Treaty of Casco (1678)
citations.quote: English settlers paid rent to the Penobscots and were given back confiscated farm land

events.notes: No copy of the treaty survives; historians rely on a 1784 summary by Jeremy Belknap. English settlers did not abide by the terms.

events.title: Treaty of Portsmouth (1713)
events.statement: On 13 July 1713 eight Wabanaki sachems signed the Treaty of Portsmouth with Massachusetts Bay and New Hampshire, ending hostilities between the Eastern Abenaki and the two provinces; the Wabanaki had not been consulted in the Treaty of Utrecht.

citations.title: Treaty of Portsmouth (1713)
citations.quote: The Treaty of Portsmouth, signed on July 13, 1713, ended hostilities between the Eastern Abenakis

citations.title: Dummer's War
citations.quote: The Abenaki signed the 1713 Treaty of Portsmouth, but they were not consulted about British ownership of Nova Scotia

citations.title: Dummer's War
citations.quote: The Treaty of Portsmouth was ratified on July 13, 1713, by eight representatives of the Wabanaki Confederacy

events.notes: The Wabanaki later objected to British readings of the treaty as an assertion of British sovereignty over their territory; no Mi'kmaq signed it or any other treaty until 1726.

events.title: Dummer's War (Father Rale's War; Lovewell's War)
events.statement: Dummer's War (1722-1725/27) pitted the New England colonies against the Wabanaki Confederacy over English expansion east of the Kennebec; Massachusetts declared war on the eastern Indians on 25 July 1722.

citations.title: Dummer's War
citations.quote: Dummer's War (1722-1725) was a series of battles between the New England Colonies and the Wabanaki Confederacy

citations.title: Dummer's War
citations.quote: Following the peace, New England settlements expanded east of the Kennebec River

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock
citations.quote: Consequently, on July 25, Shute declared war on the eastern Indians.

events.notes: End dates vary: 1725 (Wikipedia lead), 1726 (the Mi'kmaq, Maliseet and Passamaquoddy treaty ratified at Annapolis Royal on 4 June 1726) or 1727 (Penobscot timeline). Place is the Abenaki town of Norridgewock, an early target.

events.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Norridgewock massacre)
events.statement: In August 1724 about 200 New England rangers attacked the Abenaki village of Norridgewock on the Kennebec, killing the Jesuit Sebastien Rale and about eighty Abenaki, and the survivors abandoned the village and moved north to Odanak.

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock
citations.quote: Casualties, depending on the sources consulted, vary, but most accounts record about eighty Abenaki being killed.

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock
citations.quote: On August 22, 1724, Captains Jeremiah Moulton and Johnson Harmon led 200 rangers to the main Abenaki village on the Kennebec River

citations.title: Dummer's War
citations.quote: During the war, Rale was killed by a force of New England militia at Norridgewock.

events.notes: Attack dated 22-23 August 1724 (Wikipedia); casualty counts vary by source.

events.title: Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1726 (ratified at Annapolis Royal)
events.statement: On 4 June 1726 Mi'kmaw, Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet) and Passamaquoddy leaders gathered at Annapolis Royal to ratify the first Peace and Friendship Treaty with the British Crown, based on a treaty negotiated at Boston in 1725.

citations.title: The Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1726 National Historic Event - Parks Canada
citations.quote: On 4 June 1726, Mi'kmaw, Wəlastəkokewiyik, and Peskətəmohkatewey leaders gathered at Annapolis Royal, Nova Scotia, to ratify a treaty with the British Crown.

citations.title: Fact sheet on Peace and Friendship Treaties in the Maritimes and Gaspé
citations.quote: The first of the treaties was signed in 1726, formally bringing to an end a three year long war between New England and the Wabanaki.

events.notes: The Peace and Friendship treaties span 1725-1779; the 1726 treaty says little about land and did not surrender title.

events.title: Membertou baptized at Port-Royal
events.statement: On 24 June 1610 the Mi'kmaq chief Membertou and twenty members of his extended family were baptized at Port-Royal by the priest Jessé Fléché, a diplomatic ritual consolidating the alliance with the French.

citations.title: Membertou - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: on 24 June 1610, the feast day of Saint John the Baptist, the missionary priest Jessé Fléché heard the great chief's confession and baptized him

citations.title: Mi'kmaq - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In 1610, Henri Membertou, a Mi'kmaq chief (sagamo or sagamore), became the first Indigenous person to be baptized as a Catholic in New France

events.notes: The claimed 'Concordat of 1610' with the Vatican is disputed by historians and elders (The Canadian Encyclopedia). The DCB says baptism with 20 relatives; other sources say 21 or 24 relatives. Membertou died 18 September 1611 at Port-Royal.

events.title: Halifax founded by the British
events.statement: On 21 June 1749 Governor Edward Cornwallis founded Halifax on the Halifax Peninsula as the new capital of Nova Scotia, in Mi'kmaq territory; most Mi'kmaq communities refused to make peace in response.

citations.title: Halifax, Nova Scotia
citations.quote: Cornwallis founded the Town of Halifax on what is now known as the Halifax Peninsula, on June 21, 1749.

citations.title: Fact sheet on Peace and Friendship Treaties in the Maritimes and Gaspé
citations.quote: a position which they adopted in anger over the British decision to establish a new settlement at Halifax in June of 1749.

citations.title: Halifax, Nova Scotia
citations.quote: in 1749, King George II ordered Edward Cornwallis to establish Halifax as a new capital

events.title: Treaty of 1752 (Mi'kmaq of Shubenacadie)
events.statement: On 22 November 1752 Governor Peregrine Hopson and Jean-Baptiste Cope, chief sakamow of Shubenacadie, signed a treaty at Halifax reaffirming the 1726 treaty and formalizing a commercial relationship between the British and the Mi'kmaq.

citations.title: Fact sheet on Peace and Friendship Treaties in the Maritimes and Gaspé
citations.quote: This treaty was signed in Halifax on 22 November by Governor Hopson and Jean-Baptiste Cope

citations.title: Treaty of 1752
citations.quote: signed between the Mi'kmaq people of Shubenacadie, Nova Scotia and the governor of Nova Scotia on 22 November 1752

citations.title: Fact sheet on Peace and Friendship Treaties in the Maritimes and Gaspé
citations.quote: The 1752 treaty reaffirmed the 1726 treaty but also modified it by formalizing a commercial relationship

events.notes: Scholars disagree on whether Cope signed for all Mi'kmaq. R. v. Marshall (1999) upheld treaty rights from this series.

events.title: Siege of the Susquehannock fort at Piscataway Creek
events.statement: In September 1675, after leaving their Susquehanna town, the Susquehannock were besieged in their palisaded village on Piscataway Creek, Maryland, by militias from Maryland and Virginia; the survivors scattered or were absorbed by the Haudenosaunee.

citations.title: Susquehannock
citations.quote: They erected a palisaded village on Piscataway Creek, but in September 1675, the Susquehannock were besieged by militias from Maryland and Virginia.

citations.title: Susquehannock
citations.quote: The survivors of the siege scattered, and those who returned to the north were absorbed by the Haudenosaunee.

events.notes: Coordinates are approximate for the creek area.

events.title: Conestoga massacre (Paxton Boys)

place.name: Conestoga Indian Town (Manor Township, Lancaster County)

events.statement: On 14 December 1763 about fifty armed colonists from Paxton attacked Conestoga Indian Town at dawn, killing the six Conestoga found there; on 27 December they broke into the Lancaster workhouse and killed the fourteen survivors.

citations.title: Conestoga Indian Town Historical Marker - ExplorePAHistory
citations.quote: On December 14, 1763, about fifty armed colonists from Paxton (near modern Harrisburg) rode into Conestoga.

citations.title: Conestoga Indian Town Historical Marker - ExplorePAHistory
citations.quote: On December 27, the Paxton Boys returned, broke into the workhouse, and murdered the fourteen Indian men, women, and children inside.

citations.title: Paxton Boys
citations.quote: At daybreak on December 14, 1763, roughly 50 Paxton Boys attacked Conestoga Town, killed and scalped the six Conestoga they found there

events.notes: No one was ever arrested or tried (ExplorePAHistory). Total killed: 20 (Wikipedia: 6 + 14 in the workhouse, where Wikipedia says 'all fourteen of the surviving Conestoga'); one HSP source counts 21.

events.title: Beothuk leader Nonosabasut killed and Demasduit captured at Red Indian Lake
events.statement: In March 1819 settlers led by John Peyton Jr. captured Demasduit and killed the Beothuk chief Nonosabasut at Red Indian Lake in interior Newfoundland.

citations.title: Shawnadithit - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In one noted instance in March 1819, Shawnadithit observed European traders capture her aunt Demasduit and murder her uncle, Beothuk chief Nonosabasut

citations.title: Shawnadithit - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: She observed the kidnapping of Demasduwit and the killing of Nonosbawsut by Peyton's party in March 1819

events.notes: Names are spelled variously: Demasduit/Demasduwit and Nonosabasut/Nonosbawsut.

events.title: Shanawdithit, the last known Beothuk, dies at St. John's
events.statement: Shanawdithit (Nancy April), the last known survivor of the Beothuk, died of tuberculosis in St. John's on 6 June 1829; her drawings and accounts are the main record of Beothuk culture.

citations.title: Shawnadithit - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: Shawnadithit was the last known survivor of the Beothuk, the First Nations inhabitants of Newfoundland

citations.title: Shawnadithit - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Sick with tuberculosis, Shawnadithit died on 6 June 1829.

citations.title: Shawnadithit - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: While it is popularly believed that Shawnadithit was the last Beothuk, Mi'kmaq oral histories reject that claim.

citations.title: Shawnadithit - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: she was the source of much of what is known about the customs, language, and last days of her people

events.notes: The Canadian Encyclopedia notes that Mi'kmaq oral histories reject the popular belief that Shanawdithit was the last Beothuk. DCB: died 6 June 1829 in St John's; cause (tuberculosis) per The Canadian Encyclopedia and other sources.

events.title: Nanticoke move to Fort Niagara and the Six Nations (1778 onward)
events.statement: In 1778 about two hundred Nanticoke, allied with Britain, moved north to Fort Niagara and were later resettled with the Haudenosaunee at the Six Nations Reserve near Brantford, Ontario.

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: In 1778, two hundred Nanticoke moved north to Fort Niagara in present-day Canada because of their alliance.

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: Others now live on the Six Nations of the Grand River reserve in Ontario, Canada where some ancestors resettled after the Revolutionary War

events.notes: Wikipedia only.

events.title: Epidemics devastate the Wendat and neighbours (1634-1642)
events.statement: Between 1634 and 1642 a series of epidemics, particularly measles, influenza and smallpox, reduced the Wendat from perhaps 20,000-25,000 people to about 9,000.

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: between 1634 and 1642 they were reduced to about 9,000 by a series of epidemics, particularly measles, influenza and smallpox

citations.title: Petun (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A number of epidemics were documented in Huron-Petun societies between 1634 and 1640

events.notes: Range 1634-1640/42 depending on the source; the event starts in 1634.

events.title: Haudenosaunee destroy Wendake; Sainte-Marie burned
events.statement: In 1648-49 the Haudenosaunee defeated and dispersed the Wendat; on 16 June 1649 the Jesuits burned Sainte-Marie among the Hurons, the mission built within Wendake in 1639, rather than risk it being overrun, and the Wendat abandoned Wendake.

citations.title: Sainte-Marie among the Hurons (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On June 16, 1649, the missionaries chose to burn the mission rather than risk it being desecrated

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: In 1648 and 1649, armed with Dutch firearms, they defeated and dispersed the Wendat

events.notes: The Saint-Louis mission village was attacked on 16 March 1649; the Wendat soon after dispersed to Christian Island, the Petun, Quebec and the Haudenosaunee.

events.title: Pontiac's War: Odawa-led attack on Fort Detroit
events.statement: In May 1763 an alliance of Odawa, Wyandot, Potawatomi and Ojibwe under Pontiac rose against British rule; on 7 May Pontiac entered Fort Detroit with about 300 men with concealed weapons, and the fort was then besieged.

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On May 7, Pontiac entered Fort Detroit with about 300 men carrying concealed weapons

citations.title: Pontiac (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Indigenous forces laid siege to Fort Detroit.

citations.title: Pontiac (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: an alliance of Odawa, Wyandot, Potawatomi and Ojibwa ignited hostilities in the spring of 1763

events.notes: 7 May is the failed surprise attempt; the siege itself began soon after.

events.title: Royal Proclamation of 1763

place.name: Indian Reserve west of the Appalachians (Ohio River)

events.statement: Issued after Pontiac's War, the Royal Proclamation of 7 October 1763 set aside a vast Indian reserve west of the Appalachians and recognized that Indigenous nations held title to lands they occupied.

citations.title: Pontiac (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: issued by King George III on 7 October 1763, created a vast Indigenous reserve west of the Appalachian Mountains

citations.title: Odawa (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: which recognized the legal right of Indigenous communities to claim title to the lands they occupied

events.notes: Place is a representative point; the reserve ran from Georgia to the northern watershed.

events.title: Treaty of Camp Charlotte ends Lord Dunmore's War

place.name: Pickaway Plains / Scioto River Shawnee towns (Chillicothe), Ohio

events.statement: After Virginia's victory at Point Pleasant (10 October 1774), Cornstalk and the Shawnee made peace at Camp Charlotte near the Scioto towns, agreeing to cease hunting south of the Ohio River.

citations.title: Lord Dunmore's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the terms of the Treaty of Camp Charlotte (October 19, 1774), the Shawnee agreed to cease hunting south of the Ohio

citations.title: Pickaway Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The forces met on October 10, 1774, at what became known as the Battle of Point Pleasant.

events.notes: Participants listed as britain because Virginia was a British colony in 1774.

events.title: Harmar's campaign against Kekionga
events.statement: In October 1790 General Harmar's army marched on Kekionga; Hardin's detachment burned Native towns and crops, but Little Turtle's forces defeated the army in a series of battles and it retreated.

citations.title: Northwest Indian War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Harmar's advance detachment under John Hardin reached Kekionga on October 15 and spent the next few days looting and burning Native towns

citations.title: Kekionga (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: but was forced to retreat after suffering high casualties in a series of battles with forces led by Little Turtle

events.notes: Precision recorded as month.

events.title: St. Clair's Defeat (Battle of the Wabash)

place.name: Fort Recovery, Ohio (site of St. Clair's defeat)

events.statement: On 4 November 1791 a confederacy force of over 1,000 warriors led by Little Turtle, Blue Jacket and Buckongahelas overwhelmed General St. Clair's army, the most decisive defeat of a U.S. army by Native Americans.

citations.title: St. Clair's defeat (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a battle fought on 4 November 1791 in the Northwest Territory of the United States

citations.title: St. Clair's defeat (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Native Americans were led by Little Turtle of the Miamis, Blue Jacket of the Shawnees

events.title: Battle of Fallen Timbers
events.statement: On 20 August 1794 General Wayne's Legion defeated the confederacy, including Shawnee under Blue Jacket and Odawa under Egushawa, near the Maumee River in the final battle of the Northwest Indian War.

citations.title: Battle of Fallen Timbers (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Battle of Fallen Timbers (20 August 1794) was the final battle of the Northwest Indian War

citations.title: Battle of Fallen Timbers (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: it scattered the confederated Native American forces

events.title: Treaty of Greenville
events.statement: Signed at Fort Greenville on 3 August 1795, the treaty ended the Northwest Indian War; the allied nations ceded most of modern Ohio and part of Indiana to the United States.

citations.title: Treaty of Greenville (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was signed at Fort Greenville, now Greenville, Ohio, on August 3, 1795

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 further restricted them with additional land cessions to the United States.

events.title: Treaty of Fort Wayne (Ten O'clock Line Treaty)
events.statement: In September 1809 Governor William Henry Harrison obtained about 29.7 million acres in Indiana and Illinois from the Lenape, Miami, Potawatomi and others over the opposition of the Miami, Wea and Kickapoo; the treaty led to the war begun by Tecumseh and other dissenting tribesmen.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Wayne (1809) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: an 1809 treaty that obtained 29,719,530 acres of Native American land for the settlers of Illinois and Indiana

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Wayne (1809) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Miami, Wea, and Kickapoo were "vehemently" opposed to selling any more land around the Wabash River.

events.notes: Exact signing day (30 September 1809) not confirmed from a readable page; the page confirms only the September 1809 meeting.

events.title: Battle of Tippecanoe
events.statement: On 7 November 1811 Governor Harrison's army of about 1,000 attacked Prophetstown while Tecumseh was away recruiting allies; Tenskwatawa's warriors were driven off and the village was burned.

citations.title: Battle of Tippecanoe (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: fought on November 7, 1811, in Battle Ground, Indiana

citations.title: Tecumseh (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Harrison moved a force near Prophetstown at the confluence of the Tippecanoe and Wabash Rivers

events.title: Battle of the Thames; death of Tecumseh
events.statement: On 5 October 1813 the Americans defeated the British and Tecumseh's Confederacy near Moraviantown in Upper Canada; Tecumseh was killed and his confederacy collapsed.

citations.title: Battle of the Thames (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Tecumseh was killed, and his confederacy collapsed.

citations.title: Tecumseh (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: d. 5 Oct. 1813 at what is now Thamesville, Ont., in the battle of Moraviantown

events.title: Bad Axe Massacre; end of the Black Hawk War
events.statement: On 1-2 August 1832 U.S. regulars, militia and the steamboat Warrior killed Sauk and Meskwaki people, many of them unarmed non-combatants crossing the Mississippi, ending the Black Hawk War; afterward the Black Hawk Purchase took 6 million acres of Iowa.

citations.title: Bad Axe Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a massacre of Sauk (Sac) and Meskwaki (Fox) people by United States Army regulars and militia that occurred on August 1-2, 1832

citations.title: Sac and Fox (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: the event itself ended tragically with the slaughter of unarmed Thakiwaki crossing the Mississippi River

events.notes: Event dated to the second day; the fighting began on 1 August.

events.title: Treaty of Chicago (1833)
events.statement: On 26 September 1833 the Potawatomi, Odawa and Ojibwe agreed to cede about 5,000,000 acres in Illinois and Michigan Territory and to move west of the Mississippi River, the largest of the removal treaties for the Three Fires.

citations.title: Treaty of Chicago (1833) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: An initial version of the treaty was agreed to on September 26, 1833.

citations.title: Treaty of Chicago (1833) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty was one of the removal treaties to come after the passage of the Indian Removal Act.

events.notes: Supplementary articles agreed 27 September 1833.

events.title: Potawatomi Trail of Death
events.statement: On 4 September 1838 militia under Gen. John Tipton began marching about 859 Potawatomi from Twin Lakes, Indiana, to Kansas; the 660-mile journey ended on 4 November, and more than 40 people, mostly children, died.

citations.title: Potawatomi Trail of Death (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The journey from Twin Lakes, Indiana, to Osawatomie, Kansas, began on September 4, 1838

citations.title: Citizen Potawatomi (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: Known as the Trail of Death, the forced removal of the Potawatomi from the Great Lakes occurred between September and November 1838.

events.notes: Numbers removed: 859 (Wikipedia) versus 756+ (Oklahoma encyclopedia).

events.title: Forced removal of the Miami from Indiana

place.name: Miami reservation lands, Wabash River, Indiana

events.statement: Removal of the Miami rank-and-file from Indiana was to begin on 1 October 1846; it began on 6 October by canal boat, then by steamer to Kansas Landing and overland to the reservation, reached by 9 November.

citations.title: Miami people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It began October 6 by canal boat.

citations.title: Miami (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: Forced removal in 1846 resulted in half of the tribe remaining in Indiana

events.notes: Place is the Wabash valley reservation lands.

events.title: Robinson Superior and Robinson Huron Treaties
events.statement: On 7 September (Superior) and 9 September 1850 (Huron) at Sault Ste. Marie the Ojibwe chiefs of the north shores of Lake Superior and Lake Huron made the Robinson Treaties with the Crown, ceding their lands for reserves, a cash payment and annuities.

citations.title: Robinson Treaties (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was entered into agreement on September 7, 1850, at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario

citations.title: Robinson Treaties (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was entered into agreement on September 9, 1850, at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario

events.notes: Superior treaty 7 September; Huron treaty 9 September.

events.title: Battle of Mabila (de Soto expedition)

place.name: Mabila (site uncertain; Marengo County, Alabama region)

events.statement: On 18 October 1540 Hernando de Soto's expedition entered the fortified Mabila town of the chief Tuskaloosa; fighting broke out and the town was burned, with several thousand people killed in one of the bloodiest battles in early North American history.

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On October 18, 1540, de Soto and the expedition arrived at Mabila, a heavily fortified village situated on a plain.

citations.title: Hernando de Soto - Wikipedia
citations.quote: They killed an estimated 2,000-6,000 Native Americans at Mabila, making the battle one of the bloodiest in recorded North American history.

events.notes: Location debated; death estimates vary (2,000-6,000). Wikipedia only.

events.title: Battle of Ayubale in Moore's raid on Apalachee

place.name: Apalachee Province missions (Ayubale and San Luis), Florida

events.statement: On 25 January 1704 an expedition of Carolina colonists and Muscogee allies under James Moore reached the Apalachee mission town of Ayubale, during the raids that destroyed the Apalachee mission network in January 1704.

citations.title: Apalachee massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On January 25, 1704, Moore's force arrived at Ayubale, one of the larger mission towns in Apalachee.

citations.title: Apalachee massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: a series of raids by English colonists from the Province of Carolina and their Muscogee allies against a largely peaceful Apalachee population

events.notes: Coordinates are Mission San Luis, the Apalachee capital (approximate); Ayubale lay elsewhere in Apalachee Province. Wikipedia only.

events.title: Tuscarora War begins

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

events.statement: The Tuscarora War began in September 1711 when the Tuscarora Lower Towns under Chief Hancock attacked colonial settlements encroaching on their land; the war lasted until 1715.

citations.title: Tuscarora War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Tuscarora War was fought in North Carolina from September 10, 1711, until February 11, 1715

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: Hancock and the Lower Towns in September 1711 staged what was evidently intended as a warning attack on white settlements.

events.notes: Wikipedia gives 10 September 1711 for the start; NCpedia describes a surprise attack on settlers on 22 September 1711. Place = Fort Neoheroka region (Tuscarora Lower Towns).

events.title: Siege of Fort Neoheroka

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

events.statement: From 20 to 23 March 1713 a South Carolina expedition under Colonel James Moore besieged and overran Fort Neoheroka, the last great stand of the Tuscarora, ending their war-making capacity.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The last great stand of the Tuscarora took place at Fort Neoheroka on 20-23 Mar. 1713.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: This action ended the war-making capacity of the Tuscarora.

events.notes: Casualty counts differ (NCpedia: about 900 dead and captured; other sources 950-1,400).

events.title: Yamasee War begins

place.name: Pocotaligo (Yamasee town), near Yemassee, South Carolina

events.statement: The Yamasee War began on 15 April 1715 at Pocotaligo, a pan-tribal uprising against abusive trade practices that ended with the Yamasee driven from South Carolina into Florida.

citations.title: Yamasee War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The events of the early hours of Good Friday, April 15, 1715, marked the beginning of the Yamasee War.

citations.title: Yamassee War - NCpedia
citations.quote: The war began on 15 Apr. 1715 as a reaction to the abusive trade practices that white traders imposed on the Indians.

citations.title: The Muscogee Nation - Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park (NPS)
citations.quote: In 1715, the Yamasee War erupted in protest against British indignities related to the fur trade

events.notes: Participants: the Yamasee and allied peoples including Muscogee (Ochese Creek) towns and, per NCpedia, Catawba (NCpedia dates the Catawba entry to 1713, likely an error); the Cherokee first stayed neutral then joined the British.

events.title: Natchez revolt at Fort Rosalie
events.statement: On 28 November 1729 the Natchez attacked the French settlement at Fort Rosalie, killing about 230 colonists; French and Choctaw reprisals in 1730 forced the Natchez to abandon the fort and their homeland.

citations.title: Natchez revolt - Wikipedia
citations.quote: an attack by the Natchez Native American people on French colonists near present-day Natchez, Mississippi, on November 28, 1729

citations.title: Natchez revolt - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Approximately 230 colonists were killed overall

citations.title: Fort Rosalie - Wikipedia
citations.quote: French and allied Choctaw military reprisals in early 1730 forced the Natchez to abandon the fort, which was in ruins.

events.notes: The Fort Rosalie article gives 29 November 1729; the Natchez revolt article gives 28 November; used 28 November.

events.title: Battle of Ackia (French attack on Chickasaw)

place.name: Ackia and Ogoula Tchetoka (Chickasaw villages), Tupelo area, Mississippi

events.statement: On 26 May 1736 a French force from Lower Louisiana, joined by a Choctaw contingent, attacked the Chickasaw village of Ackia near present Tupelo, Mississippi, and was repulsed.
