citations.title: Battle of Ackia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: A second force from Lower Louisiana attacked Ackia on May 26, 1736.

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: such as in the Battle of Ackia on May 26, 1736

citations.title: Battle of Ackia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: before being met up-river by a 600 man Choctaw contingent

events.notes: A memoir mistakenly reported 20 May 1736 (Wikipedia). Coordinates are Tupelo (approximate).

events.title: Anglo-Cherokee War
events.statement: After tensions with encroaching settlers and mutual suspicions of betrayal, open war broke out in 1758 between the Cherokee and the British, who invaded the Cherokee homeland twice in 1759-61.

citations.title: Anglo-Cherokee War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Tensions between British-American settlers and Cherokee warriors of towns that the pioneers encroached on had increased during the 1750s, culminating in open hostilities in 1758.

citations.title: Cherokee Indians - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the British responded with two military incursions during the Anglo-Cherokee War (1759-61)

events.notes: Dates differ: Wikipedia 1758-1761, New Georgia Encyclopedia 1759-61. Fort Loudoun, besieged in 1760, is used as the place.

events.title: Treaty of Augusta confirms Catawba reservation
events.statement: At the 1763 Treaty of Augusta the British Crown confirmed the Catawba in a reservation fifteen miles square, about 144,000 acres, in South Carolina.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the 1763 Treaty of Augusta ceded the Catawba tribe of South Carolina a tract of land "fifteen miles square" comprising approximately 144,000 acres

events.notes: The South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the year only. Coordinates are Augusta, Georgia, the conference city (approximate).

events.title: Treaty of Hopewell with the Cherokee

place.name: Hopewell on the Keowee (near Pendleton), South Carolina

events.statement: On 28 November 1785 the Cherokee and the United States signed the first Treaty of Hopewell at Hopewell on the Keowee, defining the boundary of the Cherokee Nation.

citations.title: Treaty of Hopewell - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On November 28, 1785, the first Treaty of Hopewell was signed between the U.S. representative Benjamin Hawkins and the Cherokee Indians.

citations.title: Treaty of Hopewell - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The chief provision of the treaties was defining boundaries between sovereign tribal lands and lands open to settlement

events.notes: Treaties with the Choctaw (3 January 1786) and Chickasaw followed at the same place (Wikipedia). Hopewell plantation was near Pendleton, South Carolina; coordinates are Pendleton (approximate). Wikipedia only.

events.title: Battle of Horseshoe Bend (Tohopeka)
events.statement: On 27 March 1814 Andrew Jackson's army and its Cherokee and Lower Creek allies crushed the Red Stick Muscogee force at Tohopeka on the Tallapoosa River, killing at least 800 of about 1,000 warriors.

citations.title: Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1814) - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On March 27, 1814, United States forces and Native American allies under Major General Andrew Jackson defeated the Red Sticks

citations.title: History & Culture - Horseshoe Bend National Military Park (NPS)
citations.quote: By dark at least 800 of Chief Menawa's 1,000 Red Sticks were dead (557 slain on the field and 200-300 in the river).

events.notes: The Red Sticks (Upper Creeks) fought a civil war within the Muscogee Nation that began in 1813; allied Muscogee and Cherokee fought with the US.

events.title: Treaty of Fort Jackson
events.statement: The Treaty of Fort Jackson, signed 9 August 1814 near Wetumpka, Alabama, ended the Creek War and forced the Muscogee to cede 23 million acres of their land to the United States.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Jackson - Wikipedia
citations.quote: was signed on August 9, 1814 at Fort Jackson near Wetumpka, Alabama

citations.title: History & Culture - Horseshoe Bend National Military Park (NPS)
citations.quote: The Treaty of Fort Jackson ended the conflict and required the Creeks to cede 23 million acres of land to the United States.

events.notes: The cession included land of Muscogee who had been US allies.

events.title: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek

place.name: Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty site (southwest Noxubee County), near Macon, Mississippi

events.statement: On 27 September 1830 the Choctaw ceded their remaining homeland in Mississippi, over 10 million acres, to the United States in the first treaty made under the Indian Removal Act.

citations.title: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek was a treaty which was signed on September 27, 1830

citations.title: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) - Encyclopedia of Alabama
citations.quote: It was the first treaty signed after the creation of the Indian Removal Act of 1830

citations.title: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) - Encyclopedia of Alabama
citations.quote: the Choctaw ceded control of their communally held lands in central Mississippi and west-central Alabama, more than 10 million acres, to the U.S. government

citations.title: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The site of the signing of this treaty is in the southwest corner of Noxubee County

events.notes: Coordinates are Macon, Mississippi (approximate); the signing site is in southwest Noxubee County. The treaty was proclaimed 24 February 1831.

events.title: Choctaw removal begins
events.statement: The first wave of Choctaw removal from Mississippi to Indian Territory began in October 1831; more than six thousand arrived in the fall and winter of 1831-32, with great suffering from the failure to supply the march.

citations.title: A New Chahta Homeland: A History by the Decade, 1830-1840 - Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
citations.quote: The first wave of removals began in October 1831.

citations.title: Choctaw (tribe) - Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture
citations.quote: During the fall and winter of 1831-32, more than six thousand Choctaw arrived

events.notes: Place = Nanih Waiya as the homeland the Choctaw left.

events.title: Treaty of Pontotoc Creek

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

events.statement: On 20 October 1832 the Chickasaw signed the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek at their council house, ceding their remaining homeland east of the Mississippi in return for a promise of suitable land in the west.

citations.title: Treaty with the Chickasaw, 1832 (Treaty of Pontotoc Creek) - Chickasaw.tv
citations.quote: The Treaty of Pontitock Creek (also referred to as Pontotoc Creek), signed at the Chickasaw Council House on October 20, 1832

citations.title: Treaty of Pontotoc Creek - Wikipedia
citations.quote: assembled at the National Council House on Pontotoc Creek in Pontotoc, Mississippi

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: ceding their remaining Mississippi territory to the U.S.

events.notes: Chickasaw removal began in 1837.

events.title: Treaty of New Echota
events.statement: On 29 December 1835 a small group of Cherokee, the Treaty Party, signed the Treaty of New Echota with the United States, ceding the Cherokee lands in the East and agreeing to removal; the signers lacked authority under Cherokee Nation law.

citations.title: Treaty of New Echota - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Treaty of New Echota was a treaty signed on December 29, 1835, in New Echota, Georgia

citations.title: Cherokee (tribe) - Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture
citations.quote: One, known as the Ridge Party, signed the Treaty of New Echota (1835) and provided the alleged basis for tribal removal

citations.title: The History of the Cherokee Nation - Cherokee Nation
citations.quote: The Cherokees who signed that treaty lacked authority to do so under Cherokee Nation law

events.notes: Senate ratification 23 May 1836 by one vote.

events.title: Second Seminole War begins (Dade battle)

place.name: Dade battle site, near Bushnell, Florida

events.statement: On 28 December 1835 Seminole warriors defeated a US column under Major Dade south of present Bushnell, Florida, in the engagement that officially started the Second Seminole War (1835-42).

citations.title: Dade battle - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Dade battle (often called the Dade massacre) was an 1835 military defeat for the United States Army.

citations.title: Dade battle - Wikipedia
citations.quote: until December 28, when they were just south of the present-day city of Bushnell

citations.title: Second Seminole War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: This engagement officially started the war although there were a series of incidents leading up to the Dade battle.

events.notes: The war had no peace treaty; it was declared over on 14 August 1842 (Wikipedia). The Seminole wars are dated 1817-18, 1835-42 and 1855-58 (OHS).

events.title: Cherokee removal (Trail of Tears) begins
events.statement: From May 1838 about 14,000 Cherokee were forced from their homes by US troops, held in stockades and marched west to Indian Territory on the Trail of Tears; more than one-fourth of the people died in 1838-39.

citations.title: Cherokee - Great Smoky Mountains National Park (NPS)
citations.quote: In 1838, nearly 14,000 Cherokees were forced from their homes and held in stockades before beginning a grueling journey westward to Oklahoma and Arkansas.

citations.title: Cherokee (tribe) - Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture
citations.quote: In 1838-39 more than one-fourth of the tribe died on the trek from the Southeast to the Indian Territory.

citations.title: Trail of Tears - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Forcible removals began in May 1838 when General Winfield Scott received a final order from President Martin Van Buren to relocate the remaining Cherokees.

events.notes: Estimates of those removed range from about 14,000 (NPS) to over 16,000 (Wikipedia); deaths about 4,000 (Cherokee Nation) to over 4,000 (NPS).

events.title: Muscogee (Creek) removal
events.statement: In 1836-37 the US Army forced the Muscogee out of Georgia and Alabama after the Creek War of 1836; over 14,000 made the three-month journey to Indian Territory.

citations.title: The Muscogee Nation - Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park (NPS)
citations.quote: over 14,000 Muscogee Indians made the three-month journey to Oklahoma

citations.title: The Muscogee Nation - Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park (NPS)
citations.quote: The Creek War of 1836 ended when about 2,500 people, including several hundred warriors in chains, were marched on foot to Montgomery, Alabama

events.notes: Place = Tukabatchee as an Alabama Muscogee town; removal covered all of Muscogee territory.

events.title: Cherokee Nation adopts a written constitution
events.statement: In 1827 the Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution modeled on that of the United States, asserting its sovereignty; Georgia responded in 1828 by declaring the Cherokee government abolished.

citations.title: The History of the Cherokee Nation - Cherokee Nation
citations.quote: In 1827, the Cherokee Nation adopted a written Constitution modeled on that of the United States

citations.title: The History of the Cherokee Nation - Cherokee Nation
citations.quote: Georgia responded the following year by declaring the Cherokee government abolished and its citizens subject to the laws of Georgia

events.notes: The Cherokee capital was New Echota (designated 1825); the convention that wrote the constitution met in 1827. The Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) and Worcester v. Georgia (1832) cases followed.

events.title: Treaty of Medicine Creek
events.statement: On 26 December 1854 Governor Isaac Stevens concluded a treaty with the Nisqually, Puyallup, Steilacoom, Squaxin Island and related bands in which they ceded nearly all their lands for three small reservations, $32,500 and fishing and hunting rights.

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: On December 26, 1854, at Medicine Creek in present-day Thurston County, members of the Puyallup, Nisqually, Steilacoom, and Squaxin Island tribes enter a treaty

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: ceded to the U.S. in return for $32,500 and other government assistance

events.notes: HistoryLink 5253 gives ratification as 3 March 1855 while the Pierce County essay gives April 1855; not used here.

events.title: Treaty of Point Elliott
events.statement: Chief Seattle and about 80 other Puget Sound leaders signed the Treaty of Point Elliott with Governor Isaac Stevens on 22 January 1855, ceding their lands for cash, reservations and reserved fishing and hunting rights; the Senate ratified it in 1859.

citations.title: Chief Seattle and other Puget Sound leaders sign Point Elliott Treaty on January 22, 1855 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: Chief Seattle joins 81 other leaders of Puget Sound tribes in signing a treaty with Territorial Governor Isaac Stevens

citations.title: History & Culture - The Suquamish Tribe
citations.quote: The Suquamish are one of more than 20 tribal groups that were parties to the Treaty of Point Elliott, signed near Mukilteo

citations.title: Duwamish Tribe wins federal recognition on January 19, 2001 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: signed on January 22, 1855, and ratified by the United States Senate in 1859

events.notes: HistoryLink says 'Chief Seattle joins 81 other leaders' (82 signers); Wikipedia lists tribes by name. Ratified 8 March 1859 and proclaimed 11 April 1859 per Wikipedia.

events.title: Treaty of Point No Point
events.statement: On 26 January 1855 the S'Klallam, Chimakum and Skokomish ceded the northern Kitsap Peninsula and Olympic Peninsula to the United States for small reservations along Hood Canal and $60,000.

citations.title: Treaty of Point No Point - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Point No Point Treaty was signed on January 26, 1855, at Point No Point, on the northern tip of the Kitsap Peninsula

citations.title: Treaty of Point No Point - Wikipedia
citations.quote: convened the treaty council on January 25, with the S'Klallam, the Chimakum, and the Skokomish tribes

citations.title: Treaty of Point No Point - Wikipedia
citations.quote: ceded ownership of their land in exchange for small reservations along Hood Canal and a payment of $60,000 from the federal government

events.notes: HistoryLink 5402 corroborates 'four days later' (26 January) in a related agreement.

events.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic (begins at Victoria)
events.statement: Smallpox reached Victoria by steamship in March 1862 and spread north along the coast; colonial police forced Indigenous people out of Victoria (burning the Northern Encampment), and the epidemic killed an estimated two-thirds of British Columbia's First Nations people, over 70% of the Haida and 60% of the Tlingit.

citations.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic - Wikipedia
citations.quote: a major outbreak of smallpox that began in Victoria, on Vancouver Island, and quickly spread among Indigenous peoples across the Pacific Northwest Coast

citations.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The steamship Brother Jonathan arrived at Victoria on 12 March 1862 and left the next day

citations.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The death rate was highest in southeast Alaska and Haida Gwaii-over 70% among the Haida and 60% among the Tlingit

citations.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Two-thirds of British Columbia First Nations died-around 20,000 people

citations.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the police went to what remained of the Northern Encampment and burned all the dwellings

citations.title: Post-contact history - Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve (Parks Canada)
citations.quote: By the late 1800s, fewer than 600 Haida were left on Haida Gwaii

events.notes: Date conflict: the Wikipedia epidemic article gives the ship's arrival as 12 March 1862, the Haida people article says the epidemic began on 26 March. Used the dedicated article. Casualty percentages are scholarly estimates (R. Boyd) quoted by Wikipedia.

events.title: Kiks.ádi destruction of Redoubt Saint Michael (Old Sitka)

place.name: Redoubt Saint Michael / Old Sitka (Starrigavan Bay)

events.statement: In 1802 Tlingit Kiks.ádi warriors led by Skautlelt and Kotleian attacked the Russian-American Company's Redoubt Saint Michael near Sitka, killing nearly all of the Russians and Aleuts there.

citations.title: Archaeologists Identify Famed Fort Where Indigenous Tlingits Fought Russian Forces - Smithsonian Magazine
citations.quote: launched an attack on a Russian outpost near Sitka called Redoubt Saint Michael in 1802, killing nearly all of the Russians and Aleuts there

citations.title: Battle of Sitka - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In June 1802, a group of Tlingit warriors attacked the Russian fort at mid-day

citations.title: Battle of Sitka - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Led by Skautlelt (Shḵ'awulyéil) and Kotleian, the raiding party massacred many

events.notes: Month (June) from Wikipedia only; Smithsonian gives year only.

events.title: Battle of Sitka

place.name: Shís'gi Noow, Kiks.ádi fort site (Sitka National Historical Park)

events.statement: In autumn 1804 Alexander Baranov returned to Sitka with his forces; the Kiks.ádi repulsed the first assault by the Russians and Aleuts on their sapling fort but withdrew after six days when supplies ran low, and the Russians then established a fortified presence at Sitka.

citations.title: Archaeologists Identify Famed Fort Where Indigenous Tlingits Fought Russian Forces - Smithsonian Magazine
citations.quote: They successfully defended the initial assault from the Russians and Aleuts, but after six days, with supplies dwindling

citations.title: Tlingit Use of Sitka National Historical Park - Project Jukebox (UAF)
citations.quote: The park was established in 1910 to commemorate this battle and honor the fallen

events.notes: Date conflict: Smithsonian 'fall of 1804'; Wikipedia's Battle of Sitka article puts the first day on or around 1 October, its Sitka article says the fort was bombarded on the 20th (September) and abandoned on the 26th; Wikipedia's Battle article is internally dated October, used here. Duration in days varies between sources (four to six).

events.title: Treaty of cession of Russian America (Alaska Purchase) signed
events.statement: On 30 March 1867 Russia and the United States signed the treaty ceding Russian America; Article III left 'uncivilized native tribes' out of US citizenship and subject to whatever laws the United States adopted for aboriginal tribes, and the Tlingit and other Alaska Native nations were not parties to it.

citations.title: Alaska Purchase - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Seward and Steckel agreed to a treaty for the sale on March 30, 1867

citations.title: Text of Treaty with Russia - Alaska Historical Society
citations.quote: with the exception of uncivilized native tribes, shall be admitted to the enjoyment of all the rights, advantages, and immunities of citizens

citations.title: Text of Treaty with Russia - Alaska Historical Society
citations.quote: The uncivilized tribes will be subject to such laws and regulations as the United States may from time to time adopt

events.notes: 'Not parties' is inferred from the treaty text (Russia and the US only) and is not stated in the cited quotes. Wikipedia: US Senate ratified 9 April 1867. Place is Washington, D.C., where the treaty was signed.

events.title: Formal transfer of Russian America to the United States at Sitka
events.statement: American sovereignty over Alaska became legally effective on 18 October 1867, when Russian America was formally transferred to the United States in a ceremony at Sitka, on the Tlingit homeland of Sheet'ká.

citations.title: Alaska Purchase - Wikipedia
citations.quote: American sovereignty became legally effective across the territory on October 18

citations.title: Sitka, Alaska - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Sitka was the site of the transfer ceremony for the Alaska Purchase on October 18, 1867

events.notes: The US National Archives' Bureau of Indian Affairs guide gives 26 October 1867 as the purchase date (a different event); 18 October is the transfer ceremony date.

events.title: Nootka Crisis (Spanish seizure of British ships at Nootka Sound)
events.statement: In July 1789 Spain's commandant Esteban José Martínez seized British merchant ships at Nootka Sound, on Mowachaht land, setting off the Nootka Sound Controversy; Maquinna took part in the negotiations, and under the 1794 convention neither power could claim exclusive sovereignty.

citations.title: Nootka Sound Controversy - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In July 1789 Esteban Martínez, Spanish commandant at Nootka Sound, seized several British merchant ships

citations.title: Nootka Sound Controversy - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Neither nation could claim exclusive sovereignty

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Negotiations to settle the dispute were handled under the aegis and hospitality of Maquinna, a powerful chief of the Mowachaht Nuu-chah-nulth

events.notes: Santa Cruz de Nuca was founded 5 May 1789; the seizures were in July 1789 (CE).

events.title: Capture of the trading ship Boston at Yuquot (Nootka Sound)
events.statement: In March 1803 Maquinna and his warriors captured the American trading ship Boston; the captain and all the crew but two were killed, and the two survivors, including John R. Jewitt, were held captive for nearly three years.

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Maquinna and his warriors captured the American trading ship Boston in March 1803

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: He and his men killed the captain and all the crew but two, whom they kept as slaves

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: After gaining release, John R. Jewitt wrote a classic captivity narrative about his nearly 3 years with the Nuu-chah-nulth

events.notes: Wikipedia only; Jewitt's own Narrative (1815) is the primary source. Jewitt dates the ship's arrival at Nootka Sound to 12-13 March 1803.

events.title: Destruction of the trading ship Tonquin in Clayoquot Sound
events.statement: In 1811 Tla-o-qui-aht warriors attacked the American trading ship Tonquin in Clayoquot Sound after an insult by its captain; most of the crew were killed, and when a hidden crew member set fire to the magazine the explosion killed many of the warriors who had reboarded the ship.

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1811 the trading ship Tonquin was blown up in Clayoquot Sound

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The captain and almost all the crew were killed and the ship abandoned

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the resulting explosion killed many First Nation peoples

events.notes: Wikipedia only; exact day not taken.

events.title: Potlatch ban enacted in the Indian Act
events.statement: In 1884 the Canadian government amended the Indian Act to ban the potlatch, a central ceremony of the Kwakwaka'wakw and other Northwest Coast nations; the ban lasted until 1951, with confiscation of ceremonial objects and charges against participants.

citations.title: Potlatch - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the federal government banned the Potlatch from 1884 to 1951 in an amendment to the Indian Act

citations.title: Potlatch - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Authorities confiscated Potlatch items and laid charges against many people who participated in the Potlatch

citations.title: Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In 1885, the federal government enacted a law prohibiting the Potlatch

events.notes: Conflict: the Canadian Encyclopedia potlatch and Nuxalk articles say 1884-1951; its Kwakwaka'wakw article says 1885. 1884 used (the ban was in the 1884 amendment, in force 1885).

events.title: Founding of New Metlakatla on Annette Island, Alaska
events.statement: In 1887, after a dispute with the Anglican Church authorities at Metlakatla, British Columbia, William Duncan and about 825 Metlakatla Tsimshian moved to Annette Island, Alaska, and founded New Metlakatla; Congress created the Annette Island Reserve in 1891.

citations.title: Ts'msyen (Tsimshian) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In 1887, Duncan and about 825 Metlakatla Ts'msyen founded the new community of "New" Metlakatla, near Ketchikan, Alaska

citations.title: William Duncan - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: in 1887 Duncan and many Tsimshian created a second and independent Christian utopia at New Metlakatla

events.notes: Wikipedia dates Duncan's dispute and departure decision to 1886, arrival to 1887.

events.title: Pacific Fur Company founds Fort Astoria at the Columbia mouth
events.statement: In April 1811 about 33 men of John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company landed at the mouth of the Columbia and built Fort Astoria; Chinook chief Comcomly welcomed them and became a trading ally, and in 1813 the North West Company bought the post and renamed it Fort George.

citations.title: Fort Astoria - Wikipedia
citations.quote: 33 men disembarked on 12 April 1811

citations.title: Fort Astoria - Wikipedia
citations.quote: bought out the assets of the PFC in 1813, including Fort Astoria

citations.title: Comcomly (1760s?-1830) - HistoryLink
citations.quote: Comcomly was regarded as the leader of the lower Chinooks

events.notes: Landing 12 April 1811; construction of the fort followed. Site was on Chinookan (Clatsop/Chinook) land.

events.title: Intermittent fever epidemic on the lower Columbia (c. 1829-1833)

place.name: Cape Disappointment, mouth of the Columbia River

events.statement: A fever epidemic ('intermittent fever', 'cold sick', presumed malaria) swept the lower Columbia in 1829-1833 with heavy Native loss of life; Chief Comcomly died of it in 1830.

citations.title: Comcomly (1760s?-1830) - HistoryLink
citations.quote: He died in 1830, one of the many victims of an intermittent fever epidemic that swept the region

citations.title: Comcomly - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Comcomly died in 1830 after an "intermittent fever" epidemic, also called "cold sick" and presumed to be malaria

citations.title: Comcomly - Wikipedia
citations.quote: A malaria epidemic that occurred in 1830-33 in the Willamette Valley resulted in a tremendous loss of Native American lives

events.notes: Wikipedia gives an estimate of 150,000 deaths for 1829-1833 across the Willamette-Columbia confluence area, which is not independently documented here and is not used. Year given as 1830 (Comcomly's death); the epidemic ran 1829-1833.

events.title: Unangan resistance to Russian fur traders on Unalaska (1763-1766)
events.statement: From 1763 to 1766 the Unangan of Unalaska fought and attacked Russian fur traders, destroying four Russian ships and killing 175 hunters and traders.

citations.title: Unalaska, Alaska - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Between 1763 and 1766, a conflict between the Russian fur traders and the Unalaska Natives occurred

citations.title: Unalaska, Alaska - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the Aleuts destroyed four Russian ships and killed 175 hunters/traders

events.notes: Wikipedia only; the conflict is commonly dated 1763-1764 with a Russian punitive campaign to 1766; sources differ on detail.

events.title: Russian colonization of the Aleutian Islands
events.statement: By 1760 Russian fur traders had colonised the entire Aleutian chain and forced Unangax̂ hunters into the sea-otter trade, devastating their communities; by 1800 Russian presence had reached Kodiak and Southeast Alaska.

citations.title: Unangax̂ History and Culture - Aleutian Islands World War II National Historic Area (NPS)
citations.quote: colonizing the entire island chain by 1760 and expanding to Kodiak and Southeast Alaska by 1800

citations.title: Aleut - Britannica
citations.quote: Unangax people first encountered Russian colonizers in 1741

events.notes: Britannica gives first contact in 1741 (Bering expedition). 'By 1760' per NPS; a 1745 overwintering by a Russian party is also reported in other sources.

events.title: Awa'uq (Refuge Rock) massacre of Koniag Alutiiq
events.statement: In 1784 Grigory Shelikhov's company, with some 130 armed men and small cannon, attacked Koniag Alutiiq refugees gathered at Refuge Rock (Awa'uq) near Kodiak, killing hundreds, and held hostages to force Alutiiq men into sea-otter hunting.

citations.title: Archaeologist may have found site of Alaska massacre - The Seattle Times (1992)
citations.quote: In 1784, trader Grigori Shelikhov moved to end the impasse and impose the Russian will by force

citations.title: Archaeologist may have found site of Alaska massacre - The Seattle Times (1992)
citations.quote: Shelikhov sent several boats with 2 1/2-pound cannons and 130 armed men to Refuge Rock

citations.title: Refuge Rock, Partition Cove - Coastview
citations.quote: Eyewitness accounts vary but the Russians killed at least 300 men, women, and children on Refuge Rock

citations.title: Refuge Rock, Partition Cove - Coastview
citations.quote: the Russian traders enslaved men to hunt sea otters year-round, while women and children were held hostage

events.notes: Month conflict: Wikipedia August 1784; Coastview April 1784; Seattle Times only year. Death toll: Coastview at least 300; Wikipedia 200-500; Seattle Times quotes a ship physician (Britiukov) at 500 plus drownings and other accounts at 200-300.

events.title: Thule (early Inuit) migration from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland
events.statement: Around 1200 CE Thule ancestors of the Inuit moved from northern Alaska across Arctic Canada and reached Greenland by the 13th century, replacing the earlier Dorset culture.

citations.title: Early Inuit (Thule Culture) - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Early Inuit groups from northern Alaska moved into the Eastern North American Arctic (i.e., Canada and Greenland) around 800 years ago (ca. 1200 CE)

citations.title: Thule people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: They developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and expanded eastward across northern Canada, reaching Greenland by the 13th century

events.notes: Dates are approximate and vary by study (1000-1400 CE). The place is Qaanaaq in northwest Greenland, where Thule remains were first found at Comer's Midden.

events.title: Martin Frobisher meets Inuit in Frobisher Bay and takes a man captive
events.statement: In August 1576 Martin Frobisher met Inuit in Frobisher Bay, Baffin Island; five of his men were taken captive and never seen again, and before leaving Frobisher seized an Inuk who had come to his ship in a kayak and took him to England.

citations.title: Frobisher, Sir Martin - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: Just before leaving Frobisher's "strait," he captured a native who had come to the ship in his kayak to trade and took him to England

citations.title: Martin Frobisher - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On 18 August 1576, Burch's Island was sighted and named after the ship's carpenter who first spied it; there the expedition met some local Inuit

citations.title: Martin Frobisher - Wikipedia
citations.quote: five of Frobisher's men were taken captive

citations.title: Martin Frobisher - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Frobisher's men were never seen again by their fellows

events.notes: Wikipedia dates the meeting to 18 August 1576 (Burch's Island sighted 18 Aug.); DCB says 'late August'. Month precision used. Inuit oral tradition holds the sailors lived among them for some years (Wikipedia).

events.title: Hans Egede founds Hope Colony (Haabets Koloni) in Greenland
events.statement: On 3 July 1721 Hans Egede, a Dano-Norwegian priest, and about 40 colonists reached Nuup Kangerlua and began Hope Colony, re-establishing a Danish-Norwegian presence in Greenland after about 300 years and a mission among the Kalaallit.

citations.title: Hans Egede - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On 3 July they reached Nuup Kangerlua and established Hope Colony (Haabets Colonie) with the erection of a portable house on Kangeq Island

citations.title: Hans Egede - Wikipedia
citations.quote: bearing Egede, his wife and four children, and forty other colonists

citations.title: Hans Egede - Wikipedia
citations.quote: credited with revitalizing Danish-Norwegian interest in the island after contact had been broken for about 300 years

events.notes: Wikipedia's Greenlandic Inuit article: Scandinavians 'did not resettle until 1721'; in 1814 the Treaty of Kiel confirmed Greenland as a territory of Denmark. Egede's 1733 smallpox outbreak among the Inuit is described in the same Hans Egede article.

events.title: Dena'ina attack on Fort St. Nicholas ('battle of Kenai')
events.statement: In 1797 Dena'ina attacked the Russian Fort St. Nicholas at Kenai in an incident later called the battle of Kenai; more than one hundred people died on all sides.

citations.title: Kenai, Alaska - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the Dena'ina attacked Fort St. Nicholas, later dubbed the battle of Kenai

citations.title: Kenai, Alaska - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Over one hundred deaths occurred from all involved parties

events.notes: Wikipedia (Kenai article) only; the State of Alaska page does not mention the attack.

events.title: Ahtna kill the Serebrennikov party at Batzulnetas
events.statement: In summer 1848 the Ahtna killed the Russian-American Company's Ruf Serebrennikov and his entire party near Batzulnetas, ending Russian attempts to explore the Copper Basin.

citations.title: History of the Wrangell-St. Elias Area (NPS)
citations.quote: Ruf Serebrennikov and his entire party was killed by the Ahtna near the village of Batzulnetas in the summer of 1848

citations.title: History of the Wrangell-St. Elias Area (NPS)
citations.quote: The Russians appear to have made no further efforts to explore the region

events.notes: Month not stated precisely in the cited page ('summer 1848'); year precision used. The cause is not given in the cited source.

events.title: First contact with Lewis and Clark at Weippe Prairie
events.statement: In mid-September 1805 the Corps of Discovery reached Weippe Prairie, where Clark met Nimíipuu boys and then, on 22 September, the head man Twisted Hair; the Nimíipuu accepted the strangers onto their land.

citations.title: Weippe Prairie - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: In mid-September 1805, Lewis and Clark made contact with the Nez Perce for the first time.

citations.title: Weippe Prairie - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: After Lewis and Clark reunited on September 22, 1805, they spoke with a Nez Perce head man known as Twisted Hair

events.notes: Event kind "state.treaty" is used loosely for a first diplomatic contact; no treaty was made.

events.title: Nez Perce Treaty of 1855 (Walla Walla Council)

place.name: Walla Walla Valley (Camp Stevens treaty ground), Washington

events.statement: At the Walla Walla Council, Isaac Stevens and Joel Palmer concluded a treaty with the Nimíipuu on 11 June 1855 that reserved a large Nez Perce reservation (the Tribe says about 7.5 million acres) and kept the right to fish and hunt at usual and accustomed places.

citations.title: Treaty of June 9, 1863 (Kappler text)
citations.quote: supplementary and amendatory to the treaty made between the United States and said tribe on the 11th day of June, 1855

citations.title: History - Nez Perce Tribe
citations.quote: Tribal leaders negotiated retention of approximately 7.5 million acres to be protected as the Tribe's exclusive reservation.

citations.title: The Treaty Period - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: the nimíipuu agreed to cede 7.5 million acres of tribal land while still retaining the right to hunt and fish

events.notes: The 7.5 million acres is described by the Tribe as the reservation retained, and by NPS as the area ceded - sources disagree on framing. Council ran 29 May - 11 June 1855 (Wikipedia); Yakama and Umatilla/Cayuse/Walla Walla treaties were signed 9 June. Ratified 1859.

events.title: Nez Perce Treaty of 1863 ("Thief Treaty")
events.statement: After gold was found on the reservation, a second treaty council at Lapwai on 9 June 1863 shrank the Nimíipuu reservation by 90 percent; bands outside the new boundaries walked out and 51 headmen inside it made their marks. The Senate ratified it in 1867.

citations.title: The Treaty Period - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: The bands that lived outside of the proposed reservation boundaries walked out of the proceedings and refused to endorse this land grab.

citations.title: Treaty of June 9, 1863 (Kappler text)
citations.quote: at the council-ground, in the valley of the Lapwai, W. T., on the ninth day of June, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three

events.title: Battle of White Bird Canyon (opening battle of the Nez Perce War)
events.statement: On 17 June 1877 non-treaty Nimíipuu warriors defeated Captain Perry's cavalry in White Bird Canyon, the first battle of the Nez Perce War.

citations.title: White Bird Battlefield History - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: The die was cast and the first battle of the Nez Perce War began.

citations.title: White Bird Battlefield History - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: June 17, Daybreak Nimíipuu scouts kept watch on Captain Perry's column as it moved deeper into the canyon.

events.title: Battle of the Bear Paw and surrender of Chief Joseph
events.statement: After a five-day battle and siege that began 30 September 1877, about 40 miles short of the Canadian border, Chief Joseph surrendered on 5 October 1877; White Bird's group escaped to Canada.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield History - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: Following a five-day battle and siege, the nimíipuu ceased fighting at Bear Paw on October 5th, 1877

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield History - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever.

events.notes: Counts of those who surrendered vary (NPS: over 400; Wikipedia: 418). Tolo Lake, Dug Bar and the 126-day flight preceded it.

events.title: Captured Nez Perce sent to Fort Leavenworth and Indian Territory
events.statement: After Bear Paw the captured Nimíipuu were not allowed to go home to Idaho: they were taken east, held at Fort Leavenworth and then sent to Indian Territory in present Oklahoma, while others escaped to Canada.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield History - Nez Perce NHP
citations.quote: with some being sent to Indian Territory in Oklahoma, and others escaping to Canada

citations.title: Nez Perce War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: were taken prisoner and sent by train to Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

events.notes: Place = origin of the removal; the exile lasted until 1885 (Joseph's band was sent to the Colville Reservation).

events.title: Yakama Treaty of 1855 (Treaty of Yakama)

place.name: Walla Walla Valley (Camp Stevens treaty ground), Washington

events.statement: On 9 June 1855 at the Walla Walla Council the Yakama and allied bands signed a treaty with Governor Isaac Stevens ceding their lands and reserving a homeland; Kamiakin signed under duress.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: Kamiakin first refused to sign the treaty, but later did so under duress.

citations.title: Yakama Nation History & Treaties
citations.quote: Although the Treaty was signed on June 9, 1855

events.title: Yakama War begins (fight at Toppenish Creek)
events.statement: On 5 October 1855 Kamiakin's warriors and Major Haller's troops exchanged fire at Toppenish Creek, starting the Yakama War, after miners trespassed on Yakama land and the Indian sub-agent Andrew Bolon was killed.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: The fight on October 5 started the conflict that would come to be known as the Yakama (or Yakima) War.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: gunfire erupts between Yakama Chief Kamiakin's 300 warriors and Major Granville O. Haller's 84-man troop of soldiers

events.notes: Causes: HistoryLink records the Yakama elder account that miners raped and murdered Yakama women (dated "September 1955" in the essay, evidently a typo for 1855).

events.title: Killing of Marcus and Narcissa Whitman at Waiilatpu
events.statement: On 29 November 1847, during a measles epidemic that killed many Cayuse, a small group of Cayuse men killed the missionaries Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and eleven others at Waiilatpu, which led to the Cayuse War.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (1847-1850) - Oregon Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and eleven others at Waiiletpu, the Whitmans' mission near present-day Walla Walla, Washington, on November 29, 1847

citations.title: Whitman massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Cayuse in at least three villages held Whitman responsible for the widespread epidemic that killed hundreds of Cayuse

events.notes: The Cayuse call these events by other names; Oregon sources call it the Whitman murders/massacre.

events.title: Cayuse War ends with the hanging of five Cayuse men

place.name: Oregon City, Oregon (site of trial and hanging)

events.statement: After a volunteer militia campaign in 1847-48 failed to catch those responsible, friendly Cayuse gave up five men (Teloukaikt, Tomahas, Clokamas, Isaiachalakis and Kiamasumkin), who were tried at Oregon City and hanged on 3 June 1850.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (1847-1850) - Oregon Encyclopedia
citations.quote: sentenced all to a public hanging on June 3, 1850

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (1847-1850) - Oregon Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The Cayuse War ended as it had begun, with violence.

events.notes: Wikipedia dates the Cayuse War 1847-1855; the Oregon Encyclopedia 1847-1850. The place is Oregon City, where the trial was held.

events.title: Treaty with the Walla Walla, Cayuse and Umatilla (1855)

place.name: Walla Walla Valley (Camp Stevens treaty ground), Washington

events.statement: On 9 June 1855 at Camp Stevens the Walla Walla, Cayuse and Umatilla ceded 6.4 million acres and reserved the Umatilla Reservation plus off-reservation fishing, hunting and gathering rights.

citations.title: Treaty of June 9, 1855 (Kappler text)
citations.quote: by and between Isaac I. Stevens, governor and superintendent of Indian affairs for the Territory of Washington

citations.title: CTUIR - History & Culture
citations.quote: In 1855, the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla tribes and the U.S. Government negotiated a treaty

events.title: Hellgate Treaty

place.name: Hell Gate treaty ground, Bitterroot/Missoula Valley, Montana

events.statement: On 16 July 1855 at Hell Gate Governor Isaac Stevens concluded a treaty with the confederated Flathead (Salish), Kootenay and Upper Pend d'Oreille, who were to constitute the "Flathead Nation" under head chief Victor, ceding most of their lands and reserving the Flathead Reservation.

citations.title: Treaty of July 16, 1855 (Kappler text)
citations.quote: with Victor, the head chief of the Flathead tribe, as the head chief of the said nation

citations.title: Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes - New World Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The Treaty of Hellgate was signed on July 16, 1855, between Indian commissioner Isaac Stevens and the tribes located in western Montana.

events.title: Removal of the Bitterroot Salish to the Flathead Reservation
events.statement: In October 1891 Charlo and the remaining Bitterroot Salish left the Bitterroot Valley under U.S. pressure and marched about sixty miles to the Flathead Reservation.

citations.title: Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes - New World Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In October 1891, Chief Charlot and the remaining tribal members left the Bitterroot and marched sixty miles to the Flathead Reservation.

events.notes: Single non-Wikipedia source; Wikipedia (Bitterroot Salish) agrees on 1891 and says the move was forcible.

events.title: Battle of Tohotonimme (Pine Creek; Steptoe Disaster)

place.name: Pine Creek (Tohotonimme) battlefield near Rosalia, Washington

events.statement: On 17 May 1858 allied Schitsu'umsh, Spokane and Palouse warriors turned back Colonel Edward Steptoe's column near present-day Rosalia; the soldiers escaped at night.

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene Tribe
citations.quote: Known as the Battle of Tohotonimme by Tribes, the Battle of Steptoe was a conflict between several Tribes and the United States Army

citations.title: Battle of Pine Creek - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It took place on May 17, 1858, near what is present-day Rosalia, Washington.

events.notes: HistoryLink and NPS describe fighting on 17-18 May.

events.title: Battle of Four Lakes
events.statement: On 1 September 1858 Colonel George Wright's troops defeated the allied Plateau tribes at Four Lakes; four days later he won again at Spokane Plains.

citations.title: War of Aggression - HistoryLink
citations.quote: On September 1 more than 700 troops led by Colonel George Wright overwhelmed somewhat fewer than 500 Indians at Four Lakes

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On September 1, 1858, Wright's troops defeated the allied tribes at the Battle of Four Lakes

events.title: Battle of Spokane Plains
events.statement: On 5 September 1858 Wright's force defeated Native warriors on the Spokane Plains, the second of Wright's two battles against the allied Spokane, Coeur d'Alene and Palouse forces.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains occurs on September 5, 1858 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: defeat Native Americans at the Battle of Spokane Plains

events.notes: Wikipedia (Coeur d'Alene War) calls the outcome indecisive but says the tribes were greatly weakened.

events.title: Wright slaughters 800 Palouse horses at Liberty Lake

place.name: Liberty Lake area near Spokane, Washington

events.statement: On 8 September 1858 Colonel Wright ordered his troops to slaughter about 800 horses belonging to a Palouse chief, destroying the wealth and mobility of the tribes.

citations.title: Wright slaughters 800 Palouse horses - HistoryLink
citations.quote: orders his troops to slaughter 800 Native American horses (the herd of a Palouse chief) at Liberty Lake

citations.title: Wright slaughters 800 Palouse horses - HistoryLink
citations.quote: Horses represent both the wealth and military power of the tribes.

events.notes: Place is approximate: Spokane Falls point used as a regional anchor (Liberty Lake lies east of Spokane).

events.title: Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners (Hangman Creek)

place.name: Spokane Falls area (Hangman Creek / Ned-Whauld River), Washington

events.statement: From 25 September 1858 Colonel Wright hanged Yakama and Palouse prisoners he suspected of killing whites, including the Yakama leader Qualchan, who was hanged minutes after surrendering under a white flag.

citations.title: Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners - HistoryLink
citations.quote: Yakama warrior Qualchan is hanged 15 minutes after he surrenders to Wright carrying a white flag.

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the army hanged seventeen Palouse along Latah Creek which was later called Hangman Creek

events.notes: Exact site is on the Spokane-area creek later named Hangman (Latah) Creek; coordinate approximate.

events.title: Treaty of Friendship ending the Coeur d'Alene War
events.statement: On 17 September 1858 tribal nations including the Schitsu'umsh made a peace ("Treaty of Friendship") with the U.S. government after Wright's campaign.

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene Tribe
citations.quote: Treaty of Friendship September 17th, 1858 After the Battle between the Tribes and Steptoe

events.notes: Date from the Tribe's own timeline; the council was held at Wright's camp (location approximated here). Spokane leader Garry also signed a peace (HistoryLink).

events.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley
events.statement: On 1 October 1863 Governors James Nye and James Duane Doty concluded a treaty of peace and friendship at Ruby Valley with twelve chiefs of the Western Bands of the Shoshonee Nation, opening the country to travel, mail, telegraph, railroad and mining without a cession of land.

citations.title: Treaty of October 1, 1863 (Ruby Valley) - text
citations.quote: made at Ruby Valley, in the Territory of Nevada, this first day of October, A. D. one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Twelve chiefs signed for the "Western Bands of the Shoshonee Nation of Indians."

events.notes: Kappler dates the treaty 1 October 1863; ratified with amendments, proclaimed 21 October 1869.

events.title: Bear River Massacre (Massacre at Boa Ogoi)

place.name: Bear River Massacre site near Preston, Idaho

events.statement: On 29 January 1863 California Volunteers under Colonel Patrick Connor attacked a Northwestern Shoshone winter encampment of Chief Bear Hunter's people on the Bear River near present-day Preston, Idaho, killing an estimated 250 to 493 men, women and children.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: killed an estimated 250 to 493 children, women, and men at a Shoshone winter encampment on January 29, 1863

citations.title: Bear River Massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Colonel Patrick Edward Connor led a detachment of California Volunteers as part of the Bear River Expedition against Shoshone chief Bear Hunter.

citations.title: Coming to Wind River: The Eastern Shoshone Treaties of 1863 and 1868 - WyoHistory.org
citations.quote: Site of the Bear River Massacre of January 1863

events.notes: Largest recorded massacre of Native Americans by the U.S. Army; casualty estimates 250-493.

events.title: Box Elder Treaty (Northwestern Shoshone)
events.statement: On 30 July 1863, after the Bear River Massacre, the Northwestern Shoshone made a treaty with the United States at Box Elder; it had little effect until the land claim was compensated in 1968.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Box Elder Treaty is an agreement between the Northwestern Shoshone and the United States government, signed on July 30, 1863.

events.notes: Wikipedia-only item; date also listed in the Northern Shoshone article.

events.title: Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868 (Eastern Shoshone and Bannock)
events.statement: On 3 July 1868 at Fort Bridger the Eastern Shoshone (Washakie) and the Bannock concluded a treaty with the United States setting apart the Wind River reservation for the Shoshone and promising the Bannock a reservation in the Port Neuf country (Fort Hall).

citations.title: Treaty of July 3, 1868 (Kappler text)
citations.quote: Articles of a treaty made and concluded at Fort Bridger, Utah Territory,on the third day of July

citations.title: Treaty of July 3, 1868 (Kappler text)
citations.quote: which shall embrace reasonable portions of the "Port Neuf" and "Kansas Prairie" countries

citations.title: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes
citations.quote: the tribal leadership signed the Fort Bridger Treaty

events.title: Pyramid Lake War begins (Williams Station incident and the first Battle of Pyramid Lake)
events.statement: After an incident at Williams Station on 7 May 1860, Numu warriors under Numaga ambushed and defeated a volunteer force from Virginia City on 12 May 1860 near Pyramid Lake; a larger force of volunteers and regular troops fought them again on 2 June.

citations.title: The Two Battles of Pyramid Lake - Nevada SHPO marker 148
citations.quote: On May 12, 1860, Northern Paiute warriors, fighting to retain their way of life, decisively defeated a volunteer army

citations.title: The Pyramid Lake War - Pony Express NHT, NPS
citations.quote: On May 7, 1860, an incident at the Williams Station in Carson Valley, Nevada set off the Pyramid Lake War.

events.notes: Wikipedia: cease-fire August 1860, no treaty.

events.title: Wovoka's vision and the Ghost Dance of 1889
events.statement: Wovoka (Jack Wilson), a Northern Paiute prophet living in the Yerington area, said he received a vision during the solar eclipse of 1 January 1889 of the resurrection of the dead and the removal of whites; the Ghost Dance he taught spread to Plains peoples including the Lakota.

citations.title: Wovoka - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Wovoka claimed to have had a prophetic vision after falling into a coma during the solar eclipse of January 1, 1889.

citations.title: Wovoka - Wikipedia
citations.quote: it moved quickly beyond his local Paiute community by word of mouth to Native American tribes further east, notably the Lakota

events.notes: Event kind "migration" used loosely for the spread of a religious movement. Scholars give conflicting accounts of when Wovoka had his vision (Wikipedia); 1 January 1889 is the commonly cited date.

events.title: Potato War (Honey Lake)
events.statement: In the Potato War of 1857, hungry Washoe who took three acres of potatoes from a farm near Honey Lake were killed or wounded; it was the last armed conflict between the Washoe and non-Indians.

citations.title: Washoe people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The last armed conflict with the Washoes and non-Indians was the Potato War of 1857

events.notes: Wikipedia-only; kept at low confidence.

events.title: Modoc War begins (fight at Lost River)
events.statement: The Modoc War began in late November 1872 when Army troops from Fort Klamath under Major Green moved on Captain Jack's (Kintpuash's) village at Lost River to force the Modoc back to the Klamath Reservation; fighting broke out and the band withdrew to the Lava Beds.

citations.title: Modoc War - Lava Beds National Monument, NPS
citations.quote: The war lasted six months, from November 29, 1872 to June 1, 1873

citations.title: Modoc War - Lava Beds National Monument, NPS
citations.quote: The ensuing battle, the Lost River Battle, caused the Modocs to flee by boat, crossing Tule Lake, to take refuge at the Stronghold

events.notes: NPS gives both 28 November (text) and 29 November (header) for the start; 29 November used.

events.title: Captain Jack (Kintpuash) and three Modoc leaders hanged at Fort Klamath
events.statement: On 3 October 1873 Captain Jack, Schonchin John, Black Jim and Boston Charley were hanged at Fort Klamath after being convicted of the killing of General Canby and Reverend Thomas; two others had their sentences commuted to Alcatraz.

citations.title: Modoc War - Lava Beds National Monument, NPS
citations.quote: On October 3, 1873, Captain Jack, Schonchin John, Black Jim, and Boston Charley were hanged.

events.title: Federal treaty commissioners negotiate unratified treaties with California tribes
events.statement: In 1851-52 federal commissioners (Redick McKee for northern California) negotiated 18 treaties with California tribes promising about 8.5 million acres of reservations, but Congress never ratified them and did not tell the tribes.

citations.title: Tongva - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The US government signed 18 treaties between 1851 and 1852 promising 8.5 million acres (3.4 million ha) of land for reservations.

citations.title: Treaty Negotiations - Yurok Tribe
citations.quote: The Congress rejected the treaties and failed to notify the tribes of this decision.

citations.title: Redick McKee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: His party arrived on the Upper Klamath river in September 1851.

events.notes: Place is where McKee's party reached the Klamath in September 1851; the 18 treaties were signed at many sites. Wikipedia (California genocide) says none were ratified and the treaties were rejected in 1852.

events.title: Chumash revolt of 1824

place.name: Mission Santa Inés (Santa Ynez Valley), California

events.statement: On 21 February 1824, after an incident with a soldier at Mission Santa Inés, the Chumash rose at missions Santa Inés, La Purísima and Santa Barbara; they took over La Purísima and Santa Barbara, and the uprising ended in March when Mexican troops forced the holdouts at La Purísima to surrender.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Due to an incident with a soldier at Mission Santa Inés on Saturday, February 21, the rebellion began early.

citations.title: Santa Inés - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: the Chumash revolt of 1824 when the Indians aggressively protested treatment by the military guards

events.notes: California was then under the Mexican Republic.

events.title: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Dolores) founded among the Ohlone

place.name: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores), San Francisco

events.statement: On 29 June 1776 Franciscan Father Junípero Serra's mission at San Francisco was founded; Ohlone peoples were incorporated into the mission and suffered high mortality from disease.

citations.title: San Francisco de Asís - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: this mission was founded on June 29th, 1776 by Father Serra

citations.title: San Francisco de Asís - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: The mission was plagued by disease and high mortality rates among the Indian population.

events.title: Kumeyaay (Tipai) uprising at Mission San Diego

place.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá (Kumeyaay Nipawai), California

events.statement: In 1775 Kumeyaay (Tiipay) villagers, resenting mission rules, soldier abuse and punishment, attacked and burned Mission San Diego de Alcalá and killed Father Luis Jayme and two others.

citations.title: San Diego de Alcalá - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: hundreds of local Tipai Indians attacked the mission, causing great damage to the building and killing Father Jayme

citations.title: Kumeyaay - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the Tiipay-Kumeyaay villages led a revolt against the Spanish, burning down Mission San Diego and killing Father Luis Jayme along with two others

events.notes: Year only: the sources read do not give the day.

events.title: Mission San Diego de Alcalá founded on Kumeyaay land

place.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá (Kumeyaay Nipawai), California

events.statement: On 16 July 1769 Franciscan Junípero Serra founded Mission San Diego de Alcalá, the first mission in Alta California, in an area long inhabited by the Kumeyaay; the mission moved inland to the river valley in 1774.

citations.title: San Diego de Alcalá - California Missions Foundation
citations.quote: Founded by Father Junipero Serra on July 16, 1769

citations.title: Mission San Diego de Alcalá - Wikipedia
citations.quote: in an area long inhabited by the Kumeyaay people

events.notes: Wikipedia calls it the second Franciscan-founded mission in the Californias (after San Fernando Velicatá); the California Missions Foundation calls it the start of the Alta California mission chain.

events.title: Bloody Island (Clear Lake) massacre of Pomo people

place.name: Clear Lake, Lake County (Bloody Island), California

events.statement: On 15 May 1850 U.S. cavalry attacked Pomo people on an island in Clear Lake after the Pomo, enslaved and starved by the settlers Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone, had killed their captors; at least 60 Pomo were killed and an Army report claimed far more.

citations.title: Bloody Island massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: occurred on what was then an island in Clear Lake, California, on May 15, 1850

citations.title: Bloody Island massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: A number of the Pomo, an indigenous people of California, had been enslaved by two settlers, Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone

events.notes: Death toll conflicts: "at least 60" killed vs Major Sherman's July 1850 report of about 800 drowned or killed.

events.title: Mariposa War: Mariposa Battalion enters Yosemite Valley
events.statement: In the Mariposa War (December 1850 - June 1851) the state-raised Mariposa Battalion pursued the Ahwahnechee and Chowchilla; it entered Yosemite Valley on 25 March 1851, burned villages and food stores and captured Chief Tenaya.

citations.title: Mariposa Battalion - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Mariposa Battalion was a California Militia unit formed in 1851 to defeat the Ahwahnechee and Chowchillas in the Mariposa War

citations.title: Ahwahnechee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1851, during the Mariposa War, California State Militia troops of the Mariposa Battalion burned Ahwahnechee villages and took their food stores.

events.notes: Wikipedia-only. The date of first entry varies between sources (25 vs 27 March 1851).

events.title: Three Knolls Massacre of the Yahi

place.name: Ishi Wilderness / Mill Creek country (Yahi homeland), California

events.statement: In 1865 settlers attacked a sleeping Yahi group near their sacred place Black Rock on Mill Creek, killing about forty, as retaliation for the killing of three settlers; the Yahi were reduced to perhaps sixty people.

citations.title: Ishi - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1865, the Yahi were attacked in the Three Knolls Massacre, in which 40 of them were killed.

citations.title: Ishi - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It is estimated that with this massacre, Ishi's entire cultural group, the Yana/Yahi, may have been reduced to about sixty individuals.

events.notes: Wikipedia-only. Place approximate (Mill Creek country near the Ishi Wilderness).

events.title: Battle of the Big Hole (dawn attack on the Nimíipuu camp)
events.statement: During the 1877 flight, U.S. troops launched a surprise dawn attack on the sleeping Nimíipuu encampment at Big Hole on 9 August 1877; many women and children were killed as they fled. Fighting continued on 10 August.

citations.title: History & Culture - Big Hole National Battlefield, NPS
citations.quote: U.S. troops launched a surprise dawn attack on the sleeping nımí·pu· encampment on the morning of August 9.

citations.title: History & Culture - Big Hole National Battlefield, NPS
citations.quote: the battle that occurred on August 9 and 10 during the Nez Perce Flight of 1877

events.notes: The NPS page uses the Nimíipuu orthography nımí·pu·.

events.title: Malheur Reservation closed; Northern Paiute interned at Yakima
events.statement: After the Bannock War (1878) the Northern Paiute of the Malheur Reservation in Oregon were confined at Yakima, Washington, and the federal government discontinued the Malheur Reservation in 1879; Sarah Winnemucca lobbied in Washington, D.C., for their release.

events.title: California 'Act for the Government and Protection of Indians'
events.statement: In 1850 the new State of California passed the Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, which legalised the enslavement of Native Americans and let settlers capture and force them into labor.

events.title: Governor Burnett predicts a 'war of extermination' against California Indians
events.statement: On 6 January 1851 California's first governor, Peter Burnett, told the legislature that a war of extermination between the races must be expected until the Indian race became extinct, helping justify state-funded militia campaigns such as the Mariposa Battalion.
